chunks.content: Abbreviations BLIND blind uterine evacuation D&C dilatation of the cervix using surgical dilators and removal of pregnancy tissue using a surgical sharp curette or vacuum suction aspiration M/C miscarriage POCUS point of care ultrasound intermittently performed by an obstetrician RPOC retained products of conception SONO continuous ultrasound performed by a sonographer STOP surgical termination of pregnancy US ultrasound USG ultrasound‐guided uterine evacuation Key message Complication rates for blind and ultrasound‐guided uterine evacuations were similarly low. Ultrasound tended to be used in higher‐risk cases, with evidence of reduced blood loss and lower volumes of RPOC despite these cases being higher risk. 1 INTRODUCTION An average of 49 686 Australian women per year between 2019 and 2023 required surgical evacuation of gravid uterine contents, playing an integral role in management of elective pregnancy termination—abortion, postintrauterine fetal demise, retained products of conception (RPOC)—incomplete abortion, gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, , failed expectant management, or medical management of miscarriage. , Surgical evacuation offers the greatest complete evacuation rate, reduces unplanned admissions postfailed management, reduces bleeding and infection from RPOC , and decreases the role RPOC plays in the pathogenesis of infertility. , Surgical evacuation, however, has risks of hemorrhage, uterine perforation, , or uterine trauma with late sequelae of intrauterine adhesions or infertility. , To reduce the risk of surgical complications continuous ultrasound guidance (USG) during uterine evacuation (D&C) is frequently recommended to monitor procedure progress and confirm complete evacuation, , lowering rates of excessive curettage, which may cause Asherman's syndrome , and improving accuracy of tissue resection. , Ultrasound guidance can reduce operative time, rates of RPOC, infection, perforation, cervical laceration and hemorrhage. , , Traditionally, uterine evacuations are performed ‘blind’ with the experienced feel of the surgeon using vacuum suction or sharp curetting instruments inserted into the uterus without direct visualization of cervical canal or uterine cavity. , While complication rates for uterine evacuations are low and reported between 0.9% and 8.4%, preconditions potentially increase the complication risk. These include scarred cervix or uterus, , , Mullerian anomaly, , , fibroid uterus, , previous evacuation, previous unsuccessful evacuation, previous surgical termination of pregnancy (STOP) or caesarean section (CS), increasing GA and surgical inexperience. , Complication rates may improve with ultrasound guidance from experienced sonographers or obstetricians. Sonographers are highly skilled allied health professionals, qualified and experienced in real‐time image optimization, orientation, obstetric and gynecological anatomy and pathophysiology. Sonographers can provide a contemporaneous narrative of instrument position during operative procedures, dependent on visibility of the uterus seen posteriorly to an adequately filled bladder. Obstetricians can be trained to assess endometrial appearance, provide contemporaneous guidance and confirm complete evaluation using ultrasound. The study objective was to compare surgical complication rates between blind uterine evacuation (BLIND) and ultrasound‐guided uterine evacuation (USG) and assess differences in patient risk factors between groups. The study aim was to compare outcomes of ultrasound‐guided versus blind uterine evacuations in routine clinical practice. 2 MATERIAL AND METHODS This was a retrospective cohort study set in a single 750 bed private hospital in Sydney Australia with purposeful sampling of hospital records for women presenting for uterine evacuation during the period Jan 2019‐Dec 2023. Women were included if they had a clinical history of RPOC, incomplete miscarriage, STOP or adherent placenta, nonobstetric conditions were excluded. The study created two cohorts—patients receiving a uterine evacuation performed blind (BLIND) or with ultrasound guidance (USG). The USG cohort contained two subgroups with the ultrasound guidance being performed either intermittently as a Point of Care Ultrasound (POCUS) by an obstetrician or continuously by a sonographer (SONO). Data was extracted from surgical and pathology reports, patient files and admission records in the hospital database, and the ultrasound department database for referral information and imaging reports. Primary outcome data included the presence of uterine perforation, incomplete evacuation with continued RPOC, use of laparoscopy, creation of a false passage, estimated blood loss and heavy blood losses occurring during the procedure. Heavy blood loss was defined as 500 mLs or more based on the Royal College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (RCOG) postpartum hemorrhage Greentop guideline No. 52. Secondary outcome data included patient demographics and potential complication factors including patient age, BMI, gravidity, parity, gestational age, previous uterine surgery including CS, hysteroscopy, uterine evacuation or failed evacuation, previous uterine perforation, presence of fibroids or Mullerian anomaly. Surgical procedural characteristics of cervical priming, the use of either vacuum suction, forceps, sharp curettage or manual removal of RPOC and the indication for evacuation were collected from patient and obstetrician files, surgical and imaging reports. Women within the POCUS USG cohort were scanned by a C‐2‐5 MHz abdominal transducer (SonoSite X‐Porte TTC, FUJIFILM Corporation). The standard technique of one OBGYN who performed 101/132 (79%) of POCUS USG evacuations assessed uterine position before the sterile field was set up, with the transducer then left on the patient's abdomen

or failed evacuation, previous uterine perforation, presence of fibroids or Mullerian anomaly. Surgical procedural characteristics of cervical priming, the use of either vacuum suction, forceps, sharp curettage or manual removal of RPOC and the indication for evacuation were collected from patient and obstetrician files, surgical and imaging reports. Women within the POCUS USG cohort were scanned by a C‐2‐5 MHz abdominal transducer (SonoSite X‐Porte TTC, FUJIFILM Corporation). The standard technique of one OBGYN who performed 101/132 (79%) of POCUS USG evacuations assessed uterine position before the sterile field was set up, with the transducer then left on the patient's abdomen beneath the sterile field setup. The transducer was held with sterile drapes for intermittent assessment of dilators, forceps, or suction position within the uterine cavity and at the completion of uterine evacuation. The remaining eight OBGYNs performed POCUS USG evacuations with varying techniques of scanning before, during, or postprocedure. Women within the SONO USG cohort receiving continuous SONO guidance were scanned by a C‐1‐5 MHz abdominal transducer (GE Voluson E10 OLED, GE Healthcare Austria GmbH & Co OG). The uniform technique of SONO continuous guidance undertaken by all sonographers included sagittal and transverse planes for assessment of uterine position and uterine cavity contents prior to sterile setup and instrumentation. Continuous scanning was performed of the cervical canal and uterine cavity for the introduction of instruments and contemporaneous verbal assistance for direction of instruments toward RPOC and to assess completion of uterine evacuation as required. A transvaginal ultrasound (TVUS) was performed at the conclusion of surgery in the operating room if requested to assess if the evacuation of the cavity was successful. Women were only included if their obstetrician performed surgeries both blind and ultrasound‐guided in the overall study period to limit selection bias. The study included 5 years of data to allow for adequate comparative analysis. 2.1 Statistics Data analysis was performed using the Jamovi software (version 2.6; The jamovi project, 2025) and included descriptive analyses of variables reported as mean (standard deviation), median [interquartile range] or number (percentage). Statistical methods used significance at p < 0.05 using t ‐test or regression for continuous parametric data, Chi‐square or logistic regression for categorical data, and Mann–Whitney U for nonparametric data. Relative Risk (RR) and Odds Ratio (OR) were calculated with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Blood loss and gestational age were log‐transformed to address skew before linear regression analysis. Binomial logistic regression was performed for associations of surgical complication. Since all procedures were performed by 17 obstetrician gynecologists, potential clustering and nonindependence of observations were assessed using mixed logistic regression with a random intercept clustered by doctor. Mixed‐effects results are reported only when they differ qualitatively from results not accounting for clustering. This study was retrospective and exploratory in nature and was not designed around a single prespecified primary hypothesis or comparison. A range of complication outcomes with differing baseline prevalences were examined (e.g., uterine perforation, heavy blood loss, incomplete evacuation), for which different effect sizes would be considered clinically meaningful. In this context, a posthoc power calculation would necessarily require the arbitrary selection of one outcome and effect size and would not add information beyond that already provided by the effect estimates and their confidence intervals, directly conveying the precision of the estimates and the range of effect sizes compatible with the observed data, so the degree of statistical uncertainty for each outcome can be assessed. Follow up was not performed due to the retrospective cohort design. 3 RESULTS Between January 2019 and December 2023, 733 women met the inclusion criteria, with 421/733 (57.4%) BLIND and 312/733 (42.6%) USG. There were 1776 women excluded for nonobstetric conditions. Overall, the indications for uterine evacuation included: STOP 44/733 (6.0%), evacuation of miscarriage 573/733 (78.2%) and removal of RPOC 116/733 (15.8%) (Table ). Miscarriage was the main indicator within the BLIND group for 373/421 (89%) of women and within POCUS USG for 119/132 (90%) of women. For SONO USG, there were more varied indicators of miscarriage 81/180 (45%), RPOC 60/180 (33%), and STOP 39/180 (22%). Overall, gestational age at the time of procedure was first trimester 606/733 (83%), second trimester 48/733 (6.5%), and postpartum 57/733 (7.8%). Gestational ages were missing for 15/421 (2%) BLIND and 7/312 (1%) USG (Table ). The median gestational age based on indication for surgery was miscarriage 8 [7–9] weeks, STOP 12 [11–13] weeks, and RPOC 12 [8–16] weeks. All operations were performed under general anesthesia by a total of 17 consultant level Obstetrician Gynecologists (OBGYN) with experience ranging from under 2 years, 1 (5.9%); 2–5 years, 2 (11.8%); 6–9 years, 1 (5.9%); 10–14 years, 6 (35.3%); 15–20 years, 3 (17.7%); and more than 20 years, 4 (23.5%). The type of surgical equipment used during BLIND included 391/421 (93%) vacuum suction, 134/421 (32%) forceps, and 214/421 (51%) sharp curettage. Surgical

and 7/312 (1%) USG (Table ). The median gestational age based on indication for surgery was miscarriage 8 [7–9] weeks, STOP 12 [11–13] weeks, and RPOC 12 [8–16] weeks. All operations were performed under general anesthesia by a total of 17 consultant level Obstetrician Gynecologists (OBGYN) with experience ranging from under 2 years, 1 (5.9%); 2–5 years, 2 (11.8%); 6–9 years, 1 (5.9%); 10–14 years, 6 (35.3%); 15–20 years, 3 (17.7%); and more than 20 years, 4 (23.5%). The type of surgical equipment used during BLIND included 391/421 (93%) vacuum suction, 134/421 (32%) forceps, and 214/421 (51%) sharp curettage. Surgical equipment during USG included 290/321 (93%) vacuum suction, 212/321 (68%) forceps, and 117/321 (38%) sharp curettage. The manual removal of placenta without instruments was undertaken in 24/421 (6%) BLIND and 3/312 (1%) USG. Presurgical cervical ripening using misoprostol or cervagem was undertaken in 140/421 (33%) BLIND cases and 66/312 (21%) USG cases. The USG group included a subgroup of 132/312 (42.3%) women in whom ultrasound was only used intermittently during the procedure (POCUS) (Table ). One OBGYN performed 101/132 (79%) of the POCUS USGs. Eight OBGYNs performed the other 31/132 (21%) POCUS USGs. The second subgroup of 180/312 (57.7%) women had continuous ultrasound guidance performed by 14 sonographers (SONO) with a median of 15 [12–19] years postqualification. Within the SONO USG, 15 women had a TVUS in theater to assess completion of evacuation. There was no significant difference in patient age in years or BMI (Table ); however, there were differences in the gestational age at the time of procedure and indications for surgery between groups. There was strong evidence that there was a difference in range of gestational ages between groups ( U = 42 720, p = 0.0001); median gestational ages were BLIND 8 weeks [7–9], USG 8 weeks [7–11]. The 57 women with postpartum RPOC were more likely to have evacuation under USG ( x 2 (1) = 8.664, p = 0.003), OR: 2.3, CI: 1.3 to 3.9 (when accounting for clustering by obstetrician p = 0.05, OR = 2.0, CI: 1.0 to 2.8) (Table ). The proportion of postpartum women was 35/57 (61.4%) in the USG group compared with 22/57 (38.5%) in the BLIND group. The odds of USG were higher for STOP and removal of RPOC, and lower for miscarriage compared to the odds of BLIND. (Table ). Patient histories were combined as risk factors for uterine evacuation to allow for statistical analysis, including CS, pelvic surgery, previous uterine evacuation or failed evacuation, previous perforation, false passage, fibroids and Mullerian anomaly (Table ). The odds of women with risk factors for surgery being in the USG group was 1.7 times the odds of BLIND ( x 2 (1) = 12.057, p = 0.0005, OR: 1.7, CI:1.3 to 2.3). The proportion of patients with risk factors in the BLIND group was lower 136/421 (32.3%) compared to the USG group 140/312 (44.9%). All 5 patients with previous uterine perforation had continuous SONO USG. All 19 patients with previous failed BLIND were performed using POCUS USG 2/19 (10.5%) or continuous SONO USG 17/19 (89.5%). SONO USG was also used for completion of evacuation after one BLIND perforation, guidance for one insertion of foley catheter and Bakri balloon for two patients with heavy blood losses. 3.1 Complication rate Of the 733 women, 46/733 (6.3%) women experienced a surgical complication. In the BLIND group there were 23/421 (5.5%) women and in the USG group there were 23/312 (7.3%) women with complications, with no association between group and surgical complication ( x 2 (1) = 1.110, p = 0.292) (when accounting for clustering by Obstetrician p = 0.065, OR = 0.53, CI: 0.27 to 1.04) (Table ). There was evidence of an association between complicated surgery and gestational age ( U = 5801, p = 0.0001). The median gestational age for noncomplicated surgeries was 8 weeks [7–9] and the median gestational age for complicated surgeries was 10 weeks [9–13]. The 15 patients with missing gestational ages were all uncomplicated. While holding gestational age constant, the odds of a complication in USG were similar to the odds of BLIND, OR: 1.0, CI: 0.5 to 2.0. There was strong evidence of an association between complicated surgery and patients who were postpartum ( x 2 (1) 6.726, p = 0.010). Although numbers were small, the proportions of postpartum complications in each group were BLIND 4/22 (18%) and USG 5/35 (14%). The four postpartum complications in the BLIND group all had heavy blood loss immediately postnormal vaginal delivery (NVD) with manual removal of placenta. The five postpartum USG complications included four with blood loss: one woman immediately post‐NVD, two women 2–6 weeks post‐NVD, one woman 6 weeks post‐CS, and one uterine perforation under suction and sharp curettage. However, there was no evidence of an association

between complicated surgery and patients who were postpartum ( x 2 (1) 6.726, p = 0.010). Although numbers were small, the proportions of postpartum complications in each group were BLIND 4/22 (18%) and USG 5/35 (14%). The four postpartum complications in the BLIND group all had heavy blood loss immediately postnormal vaginal delivery (NVD) with manual removal of placenta. The five postpartum USG complications included four with blood loss: one woman immediately post‐NVD, two women 2–6 weeks post‐NVD, one woman 6 weeks post‐CS, and one uterine perforation under suction and sharp curettage. However, there was no evidence of an association between complicated surgery and previous CS ( x 2 (1) 0.8449, p = 0.358), previous uterine surgery ( x 2 (1) 0.056, p = 0.813), previous evacuation ( x 2 (1) 0.746, p = 0.388), Mullerian anomaly ( x 2 (1) 0.134, p = 0.715), or fibroids ( x 2 (1) 0.055, p = 0.815). The uterine perforation rate was 3/733 (0.4%). There were two BLIND perforations, both recognized at the time of surgery; one proceeded to be completed under laparoscopic guidance, showing no bowel perforation, and one proceeded to USG SONO. There was one perforation under POCUS USG, discovered postsurgically by pathological fimbrial tissue. The patient was later readmitted for laparoscopy, showing sigmoid epiploica and left tube within the left uterine cornua without bowel perforation. There were no perforations in the USG SONO continuous guidance subgroup. There were no instrumental false passages recorded in either group. The incomplete evacuation rate with persistent RPOC was 23/733 (3.1%). Women had similar prevalence of incomplete evacuation in BLIND 14/421 (3.33%) and USG 9/312 (2.88%), RR = 1.0, CI: 0.97 to 1.02, p = 0.74. However, there was evidence ( U = 23, p = 0.019) that the volume of persistent RPOC measured in 3 planes (cm 3 ), was larger in BLIND 8.35 cm 3 [1.49–18.94] compared to USG 0.66 cm 3 [0.53–1.23]. (Supplementary 1) The following clinical symptoms elicited an ultrasound to diagnose RPOC after evacuation; prolonged or excessive bleeding ( n = 9), pain without bleeding ( n = 5), no return of menstrual cycle ( n = 3), scan by obstetrician ( n = 3), negative pathology ( n = 1), known RPOC at the end of evacuation ( n = 1) and unknown ( n = 1). Ultrasound criteria used to define RPOC included a focally thickened heterogenous endometrium or endometrial mass exhibiting vascularity when scrutinized with Doppler which dramatically increases the diagnostic confidence for identifying RPOC. There was evidence of an association between gestational age and continued RPOC ( x 2 (1) = 5.274, p = 0.022). Within USG the following technical factors that obscured visualization of the uterus were observed to potentially contribute to continued RPOC; an empty bladder ( n = 1), bowel obscuring uterine fundus ( n = 1), blood filled cavity ( n = 1) and small RPOC in the cornua ( n = 2). There was strong evidence of association between group and use of forceps during surgery ( x 2 (1) = 93.809, p = <0.0001), BLIND 134/421 (32%) and USG 212/312 (68%). The odds of forceps use in USG was 4.5 times more likely than the odds in BLIND (CI: 3.3 to 6.2). There was no evidence of a difference in the proportion of repeat surgery rate between groups ( x 2 (1) = 0.857, p = 0.355). The prevalence of repeat surgery was 1.6 times higher in BLIND, OR 1.6, CI: 0.5–4.8. Within BLIND, 11/421 (2.6%) women had a successful repeat evacuation, 6 performed by hysteroscope, 3 by ultrasound‐guided hysteroscope and 2 by USG SONO. Within USG, 5/312 (1.6%) women had successful repeat surgery, one performed by hysteroscope and four by USG SONO. The rate of heavy blood loss over 500 mLs was 20/733 (2.7%), which included 7 BLIND and 13 USG women. There was evidence of an association between increasing gestational age and mean blood loss ( t (607) = 10.95, p < 0.001). On average, blood loss increased by a factor of 18% for every 10% increase in gestational age (CI: 15% to 21% increase). There was evidence ( U = 53 190, p = 0.047) that overall estimated blood loss was less in USG 20 mL [10–59] compared to BLIND 30 mL [10–53]. There was no evidence of association between the amount of heavy blood loss (mL) and group ( U = 34, p = 0.376). Median heavy blood loss was 1000 mL [550–1600] in the BLIND group and 800 mL [500–1000] in the USG group. There was no evidence of association between group and blood loss complication ( x 2 (1) = 2.625, p = 0.105). The median gestational age for 9 women with heavy blood loss in USG was 13 weeks [11–19] and for

overall estimated blood loss was less in USG 20 mL [10–59] compared to BLIND 30 mL [10–53]. There was no evidence of association between the amount of heavy blood loss (mL) and group ( U = 34, p = 0.376). Median heavy blood loss was 1000 mL [550–1600] in the BLIND group and 800 mL [500–1000] in the USG group. There was no evidence of association between group and blood loss complication ( x 2 (1) = 2.625, p = 0.105). The median gestational age for 9 women with heavy blood loss in USG was 13 weeks [11–19] and for 3 women in BLIND was 10 weeks [9–14]. There were 4 postpartum women with blood loss complications in each group, one patient in BLIND proceeded to uterine embolization and subtotal abdominal hysterectomy. 4 DISCUSSION This study highlighted low complication rates for uterine evacuation when performed blind or with ultrasound guidance. Ultrasound guidance was selected for patients with previous complications and preferred for STOP and RPOC cases, which included higher gestational ages and postpartum women. There was a lower volume of retained tissue postprocedure in the US group. The overall study complication rate was low at 6.3% (Table ), similar to the 6% complication rate suggested when obtaining consent from women undergoing surgical management of miscarriage and RPOC. The uterine perforation rate of 0.4% was within the range 0.1%–1.5% reported by RCOG. Reporting of perforation can be dependent on diagnosis being made during surgery, the patient having post‐surgical symptoms or indicated by pathology results, as was the case with one POCUS USG perforation. This highlights that intermittent assessment of instruments within the cavity (POCUS) is not equivalent to the continuous vision and guidance offered by the SONO group. Binomial logistic regression analysis found the only variables associated with a complication were gestational age and the postpartum state. Our results differ from the findings of Levin, who found intraoperative ultrasound guidance during the second trimester, the only independent factor positively associated with the occurrence of an adverse outcome. Similar to Shakir's study, our results demonstrated blood loss increased with increasing gestational age. As our study included 606/733 (83%) first‐trimester gestational ages, our results were similar to Acharya and Elsayed, who found that ultrasound guidance at first‐trimester STOP reduced overall blood loss, with average blood loss significantly less in our USG group. In addition, our study rate of significant hemorrhage (blood loss more than 500 mL) was equal for ultrasound‐guided and blind evacuations, consistent with Acharya. Ultrasound guidance was preferred for STOP and RPOC. Guidance can be performed according to obstetrician custom and practice rather than case selection, however, our study found USG was more likely chosen for patients with risk factors for evacuation. Previous studies reported only the presence of fibroids, , previous STOP, previous CS, and one study excluded women with previous uterine scars or surgery. In our study, ultrasound guidance was used for all patients with previous perforation or failed blind evacuation, to support after blind complication or assist the insertion of a foley catheter or Bakri balloon for blood loss management. Ultrasound guidance was successful for all our repeat surgical evacuation of the uterus for women with incomplete evacuation. Australian guidelines state vacuum suction is conditionally recommended as the preferred surgical procedure for miscarriage under 14 weeks and that dilatation and sharp curettage is preferentially avoided. A low grade of evidence suggests sharp curettage is associated with an increased risk of intrauterine adhesions. Based on our findings, the use of vacuum suction alone, sharp curettage, or a combination of both followed the surgeon's preference (Table ) The ongoing selective use of sharp curettage in our department highlights the need for larger prospective studies to evaluate infrequent or long‐term outcomes. The ability of ultrasound guidance to direct forceps to the exact position of RPOC could explain the higher forceps use in the USG cohort (Table ). Ultrasound guidance does significantly increase the amount of RPOC removed; however, it does have limitations. Our study concurs with Maslovitz, that it is not uncommon to find residual tissue after surgical evacuation. There were 14 women with continuing RPOC within BLIND and 9 women within USG. Larish suggested an implementation of transvaginal ultrasound as an effective safety check to confirm complete uterine evacuation following surgery. One patient with a history of 4 previous D&Cs underwent SONO USG, including transvaginal ultrasound in theater at the completion of surgery, and was found to have a small necrotic RPOC within the right cornua on sonohysterogram 9 weeks later. This suggests that, although transvaginal ultrasound is a very useful tool to check completion, small amounts of RPOC can be obscured by blood within the cavity or be difficult to detect within the uterine cornua. Further research is needed to assess the effectiveness of transvaginal ultrasound during uterine evacuations.

This suggests that, although transvaginal ultrasound is a very useful tool to check completion, small amounts of RPOC can be obscured by blood within the cavity or be difficult to detect within the uterine cornua. Further research is needed to assess the effectiveness of transvaginal ultrasound during uterine evacuations. The availability of USG in this study was utilized to support higher risk surgeries, with obstetricians preferring to perform STOP and removal of RPOC under USG. Therefore, training of obstetricians and gynecologists, sonographers, and health care assistants should be considered, given the evidence of improved patient outcomes for both routine and higher risk surgeries. The success of surgical evacuation may be influenced by GA, and as our study demonstrated, increasing GA increases blood loss and incidence of RPOC, indicating ultrasound guidance would be valuable for surgeries in later gestations. A higher prevalence of repeat surgery within the BLIND group could potentially be explained by larger residual RPOC volumes after BLIND was performed. Trauma to the uterine lining during D&C is implicated in the formation of intrauterine adhesions which are associated with pain, placental implantation disorders and decreased fertility. An USG evacuation can improve reproductive outcomes, reduce excessive curettage and minimize unnecessary trauma to the endometrium. Ben Ami found the presence of residual trophoblastic tissue rather than surgical intervention in the gravid uterus is primarily related to RPOC‐associated infertility. The reduction in residual RPOC could therefore be crucial for a woman's fertility. Hysteroscopic assessment for adhesions 4–8 weeks after D&C has been suggested to further understand patient outcomes after ultrasound‐guided curettage. However, appearances of the uterine cavity and endometrial disruptions on transvaginal ultrasound can be preferably used to assess intrauterine adhesions without the need for hysteroscopy. The strengths of this study included access to extensive imaging data from a dedicated women's imaging department run by obstetrician gynecologists specializing in ultrasound and detailed surgical and patient history data from obstetricians within a maternity hospital. This study was set in a large private hospital, highlighting the benefit of access to ultrasound machines, trained sonographers, and experienced obstetricians. Review of outcomes at differently sized facilities and training hospitals may highlight differing complication rates of less experienced POCUS USG and availability of SONO USG. The retrospective, nonrandomized design means that ultrasound guidance was preferentially used in selected cases, introducing selection bias, and limiting full comparability between the BLIND and USG groups. Future studies should be adequately powered to definitively comment on statistically significant complication rates. For some particularly rarer complications such as uterine perforation, laparoscopy and heavy blood loss which is affected by gestational age, the confidence intervals are relatively wide, indicating limited power to detect small group relative differences. A potential confounder of surgical inexperience for uterine perforation was not a factor in our study; , however, variability in ultrasound operator experience could impact comparability between groups. Outcomes may differ in other hospital settings due to surgical training levels, access to ultrasound equipment and trained sonographers available to assist. This study did not evaluate postprocedure infection or surgical time. Lastly, a key limitation of the study is that blind procedures have a higher risk of unreported or unrecognized false passages and perforations. 5 CONCLUSION Despite being more commonly used in patients with more advanced gestational age and higher surgical risk, ultrasound guidance was associated with reduced estimated blood loss and a lower volume of RPOC. Overall, there were low complication rates for evacuation performed BLIND or USG; however, blind evacuations have the potential for unrecognized and unreported false passages or perforation. Ultrasound guidance is a compelling choice for patients with previous complications, higher gestational ages, postpartum RPOC, or repeat surgeries. Future studies on the availability of sonographer or obstetrician guidance are warranted to address gaps in service provision and improve patient outcomes. documents.title: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome

chunks.content: 1 Introduction Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is the most common endocrine and metabolic disorder affecting women of reproductive age, with an estimated global prevalence of 5% to 20% ( , ). This condition is defined by three cardinal clinical manifestations: hyperandrogenism, persistent anovulation, and the presence of polycystic ovarian morphology. These pathological states are primary contributors to infertility, insulin resistance (IR), obesity, and cardiovascular complications, severely impacting both reproductive health and overall quality of life ( , ). Critically, PCOS is now recognized as a systemic condition characterized by chronic inflammation, dysregulated steroidogenesis, and autoimmune features, exerting long-term, systemic effects ( ). A substantial body of clinical evidence indicates that individuals with PCOS face a significantly elevated long-term risk of endometrial cancer, developing type 2 diabetes, metabolic syndrome, and cardiovascular disease ( , ). Therefore, elucidating the pathogenesis of PCOS and identifying more effective and safer therapeutic strategies are of paramount scientific and clinical importance for safeguarding women’s health across their lifespan. The pathophysiology of PCOS is exceedingly complex, wherein chronic low-grade inflammation and insulin resistance (IR) are considered two core, intertwined drivers that create a vicious cycle ( , ). Studies have demonstrated that levels of various pro-inflammatory cytokines are abnormally elevated in PCOS patients, particularly Tumor Necrosis Factor-alpha (TNF-α), which not only acts as a key mediator of the inflammatory response but also plays a crucial regulatory role within the local ovarian microenvironment ( , ). Elevated levels of TNF-α are also strongly associated with hyperandrogenism and IR in these patients ( , ). IR is defined by a diminished biological response of target cells to normal insulin concentrations. The Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase/Protein Kinase B (PI3K/Akt) signaling pathway is a principal downstream cascade that mediates insulin’s critical functions, including cell proliferation, differentiation, metabolism, and survival ( , ). A growing body of evidence suggests that pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α can interfere with the phosphorylation of insulin receptor substrates, thereby inhibiting the proper activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway ( ). It should be emphasized that this study focuses on TNF-α-centered inflammatory signaling within granulosa cells rather than a comprehensive immune cell–mediated inflammatory network. While PCOS is a systemic immune-metabolic disorder, granulosa cell–derived cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-6 represent critical local inflammatory drivers within the ovarian microenvironment. Accordingly, the present work is intentionally scoped to a granulosa cell–intrinsic, cytokine-centered mechanism under metabolic stress, rather than systemic endocrine–immune regulation or immune-cell–driven inflammatory networks in vivo . Current clinical management of PCOS is largely symptomatic, relying on treatments such as oral contraceptives to regulate menstrual cycles and reduce androgen levels, or insulin sensitizers like metformin to ameliorate metabolic disturbances. While these approaches can alleviate clinical symptoms to some extent, they often fail to address the fundamental pathology of the disease ( , ). In this context, Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM), characterized by its holistic, multi-component, and multi-target approach, is gaining global attention as a complementary and alternative therapy for various complex conditions, ranging from cancer pain management ( ) to metabolic and reproductive disorders. Gui Shen Wan (GSW) is a classic formula derived from ancient Chinese medical texts, traditionally used to restore ovarian function ( ). Because kidney-deficiency patterns in TCM are often based on chronic inflammation and immune dysregulation as its biological foundation, GSW is hypothesized to possess potential anti-inflammatory properties that warrant investigation. However, its modern pharmacological mechanisms for treating complex diseases like PCOS remain largely uncharacterized and lack high-quality scientific evidence. Notably, other classical formulas for gynecological disorders, such as Guizhi Fuling Wan, have been demonstrated to treat PCOS through mechanisms involving anti-inflammation and improvement of insulin resistance ( – ). This suggests that GSW may possess similar therapeutic potential that warrants in-depth investigation. Granulosa cell dysfunction represents a key cellular basis of PCOS-associated inflammation and endocrine dysregulation, making it a suitable in vitro system to dissect cytokine-driven signaling mechanisms. This study was designed to clarify the potential molecular mechanisms underlying the therapeutic effects of GSW on PCOS. By integrating network pharmacology to identify the common targets between the serum-absorbed components of GSW and PCOS, we predicted key pathways for subsequent in vitro validation. Our central hypothesis was that GSW alleviates the inflammatory state in PCOS granulosa cells. We posited this occurs through the downregulation of both the expression and secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-α. This anti-inflammatory effect, subsequently removes the inhibitory pressure on the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, restoring its proper function and ultimately ameliorating the dysregulation of cell proliferation, apoptosis, and hormone secretion. Furthermore, this study investigates embelin and nobiletin, key active components of GSW, to determine if they exhibit similar therapeutic effects. These findings provide a solid experimental basis for the clinical application of GSW and offer new insights into target development for PCOS therapy. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Animals and preparation of medicated

This anti-inflammatory effect, subsequently removes the inhibitory pressure on the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway, restoring its proper function and ultimately ameliorating the dysregulation of cell proliferation, apoptosis, and hormone secretion. Furthermore, this study investigates embelin and nobiletin, key active components of GSW, to determine if they exhibit similar therapeutic effects. These findings provide a solid experimental basis for the clinical application of GSW and offer new insights into target development for PCOS therapy. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Animals and preparation of medicated serum All animal experiments were conducted in strict accordance with international guidelines for animal care and use and received approval from the Quanzhou Medical College Experimental Animal Ethics Committee (Approval Number 2024049). This investigation utilized a total of 18 female rats (age: 6 weeks) of the Sprague-Dawley (SD) strain. These animals were supplied by Sipeifu (Beijing) Biotechnology Co., Ltd., which operates under the animal license SCXK(Jing) 2024-0001. Following a 5-day acclimatization period, a randomization process was utilized to allocate the subjects into three distinct experimental arms, with each arm comprising six animals: a control group receiving vehicle, a positive control group treated with 0.2 mg/kg Ethinylestradiol/Cyproterone acetate and 0.23 g/kg Metformin, and the GSW group, which was administered Gui Shen Wan. The formula consists of Cuscutae Semen (Tu Si Zi), Eucommiae Cortex (Du Zhong), Lycii Fructus (Gou Qi Zi), Angelicae Sinensis Radix (Dang Gui), Corni Fructus (Shan Zhu Yu), Rehmanniae Radix Praeparata (Shu Di Huang), Dioscoreae Rhizoma (Shan Yao), and Poria (Fu Ling). The final aqueous extract was concentrated to 1 g crude drug/mL. It was administered at a dosage of 0.1 mL/100g, prepared by the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine. All treatments were administered once daily via oral gavage for seven days. One hour after the final administration, all rats were anesthetized, and blood samples were collected under sterile conditions from the abdominal aorta for subsequent analysis. To isolate the serum, collected blood samples were initially allowed to clot at room temperature stand for 3 hours. Following this, the specimens were subjected to a 15-minute centrifugation step, applying a rotational speed of 3,000 rpm. The serum collected from rats within the same experimental group was then pooled and processed. The protocol required a 30-minute incubation at 56 °C within a water bath to achieve heat inactivation. Directly afterward, the serum underwent sterile filtration by passing it through a 0.22 µm micropore filter. The resulting medicated serum was then dispensed into aliquots and stored at -80 °C. Medicated serum from the ethinylestradiol/cyproterone acetate plus metformin group was used as a pharmacological reference reflecting commonly used clinical management for PCOS-associated endocrine and metabolic dysregulation. 2.2 UPLC-MS/MS analysis of serum bioactive components To analyze the bioactive components in the GSW-medicated serum, sample preparation was first conducted. This involved precipitating serum proteins with an acetonitrile/methanol solution, after which the supernatant was collected by centrifugation. This analysis was performed on a UPLC-MS/MS system (ExionLC™ AD, SCIEX). Chromatographic separation was carried out on an Agilent SB-C18 column (1.8 µm, 2.1 mm × 100 mm), utilizing a gradient elution. The mobile phase was composed of 0.1% formic acid in water and acetonitrile. For detection, the mass spectrometry analysis was operated in both positive and negative electrospray ionization (ESI) modes. Metabolite identification was based on fragmentation patterns matched against a self-built database, and quantification was performed in Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) mode by integrating chromatographic peak areas. 2.3 Network pharmacology analysis To elucidate GSW’s underlying mechanisms against PCOS, a strategy based on network pharmacology was employed. Specifically, the bioactive components identified in the GSW-medicated serum via UPLC-MS/MS served as the candidate library for this analysis. Initially, candidate active constituents were screened using pharmacokinetic parameters, specifically oral bioavailability (OB) ≥ 30% and a drug-likeness (DL) score ≥ 0.18. Putative targets for the selected compounds were subsequently predicted via the TCMSP, SwissTargetPrediction, and SymMap platforms. All retrieved target proteins underwent normalization against the UniProt knowledgebase. Concurrently, targets related to PCOS pathogenesis were aggregated from the GeneCards and OMIM resources. GSW’s primary therapeutic targets for PCOS were pinpointed by intersecting the set of drug-related targets with the disease-specific targets. An integrated “drug-component-target” map was thereafter generated and graphically rendered using Cytoscape software (v3.7.2). For a deeper analysis of the interplay among these core targets, a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network was constructed utilizing information from the STRING database (requiring an interaction score > 0.4). Central (hub) genes within this network were pinpointed via the CytoHubba plugin, integrating the consensus results from five distinct algorithms (MCC, MNC, Degree, EPC, and BottleNeck). Finally, to investigate the pertinent biological functions and signaling cascades, Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment evaluations were performed. Finally, to investigate the pertinent biological functions and signaling cascades, Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway enrichment evaluations were performed. These functional annotations were carried out using the DAVID 6.8 platform, with a P-value < 0.05 set as the criterion for statistical significance. Although these constituents were detected in medicated serum, OB/DL thresholds were applied as a standardized prioritization strategy in network pharmacology; this may bias toward compounds with higher predicted drug-like properties. 2.4 Cell culture and PCOS model The human granulosa cell line KGN was cultured in DMEM/F-12 medium (Gibco, Cat. No. 11320033) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS; Gibco, 10099141) and 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco, 15140122). The cells were maintained in a humidified incubator (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Heracell™ VIOS 160i) at 37°C with an atmosphere of 5% CO 2 . To establish an in vitro PCOS model, KGN cells were seeded into culture plates and grown to 70-80% confluency. Subsequently, the culture medium was replaced with a medium containing 1 µmol/L dexamethasone (Sigma-Aldrich, D4902) and 100 nmol/L insulin (Sigma-Aldrich, I9278), and the cells were incubated for an additional 48 hours to induce a PCOS-like cellular phenotype before subsequent treatments. This dexamethasone- and insulin-induced system was used to model key PCOS-relevant cellular features (inflammation, impaired PI3K/Akt activation, apoptosis, and steroidogenic dysregulation) under metabolic stress, rather than to recapitulate the full systemic endocrine–immune phenotype of PCOS. Unlike other ovarian cell lines, KGN cells retain key physiological granulosa cell characteristics, including functional follicle-stimulating hormone receptors and aromatase activity, making them a valid model for investigating steroidogenic and inflammatory responses ( , ). Model establishment was verified by increased apoptosis and inflammatory cytokine production, together with reduced PI3K/Akt phosphorylation in the Model group, as shown in the Results. 2.5 Experimental group design For the primary efficacy assessment, cells were divided into six groups: a control group treated with blank serum (Control); a model group treated with model serum (Model); a positive control group treated with Ethinylestradiol/Cyproterone acetate + Metformin-medicated serum (Ethinylestradiol/Cyproterone acetate + Metformin); and three experimental groups treated with low (5%), medium (10%), and high (20%) doses of GSW-medicated serum (Low-dose, Mid-dose, and High-dose), respectively. To investigate the causal relationship between inflammation and PI3K/Akt signaling, a mechanism-rescue experiment was performed with the following groups: Control, Model, Model + 20 ng/mL recombinant human TNF-α (TNF-α, PeproTech, 300-01A), Model cells + high-dose GSW serum (GSW), and Model cells + high-dose GSW serum + recombinant human TNF-α (GSW + TNF-α). For the validation of key active components, model cells treated with 15 μM embelin (Low-embelin), 30 μM embelin (High-embelin), 10 μM nobiletin (Low-nobiletin), 20 μM nobiletin (High-nobiletin) or a combination of 15 μM embelin and 10 μM nobiletin (embelin+nobiletin). The concentrations of these monomers were determined based on previous studies ( , ). Embelin and nobiletin were procured from MedChemExpress under the product codes HY-N0115 and HY-N0145, respectively. For monomer treatments, compounds were dissolved in DMSO, and vehicle controls containing the same final DMSO concentration were included in all experiments. 2.6 Cell viability assay The evaluation of cellular viability was conducted using the Cell Counting Kit-8 (CCK-8) assay (Dojindo, CK04). Initially, KGN cells were dispensed into 96-well plates, with each well containing 3.5 × 10 3 cells suspended in 100 µL of medium. This was followed by a 24-hour incubation period, allowing cells to adhere and reach approximately 60% confluence. Subsequent to this, the cultures were exposed to differing concentrations of medicated serum for an additional 24-hour duration. Upon completion of the treatment incubation, every well received 10 µL of freshly diluted CCK-8 solution. A final 2-hour incubation of the plates was performed at 37°C, ensuring they were protected from light. Finally, to quantify cell viability, the optical density was recorded at 450 nm utilizing a BIOBASE-EL10A microplate reader. 2.7 Apoptosis assay For every sample, an aliquot of approximately 1 × 10 6 cells was gathered. The cells underwent two washing cycles with ice-cold PBS (Gibco, 10010023) and were subsequently pelleted via centrifugation (1500 rpm, 3 min). The resulting cellular pellet was resuspended within 300 µL of cold 1× Binding Buffer. A staining solution, consisting of 5 µL of Annexin V-FITC and 10 µL of Propidium Iodide (PI), was then introduced to the cell suspension. After gentle mixing, the mixture was incubated for 10 minutes at ambient temperature while shielded from light. In the final

a BIOBASE-EL10A microplate reader. 2.7 Apoptosis assay For every sample, an aliquot of approximately 1 × 10 6 cells was gathered. The cells underwent two washing cycles with ice-cold PBS (Gibco, 10010023) and were subsequently pelleted via centrifugation (1500 rpm, 3 min). The resulting cellular pellet was resuspended within 300 µL of cold 1× Binding Buffer. A staining solution, consisting of 5 µL of Annexin V-FITC and 10 µL of Propidium Iodide (PI), was then introduced to the cell suspension. After gentle mixing, the mixture was incubated for 10 minutes at ambient temperature while shielded from light. In the final preparation step, an additional 200 µL of cold 1× Binding Buffer was dispensed into each sample. Prompt analysis was then performed by flow cytometry using a FACSCanto II instrument (BD Biosciences). 2.8 Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay The concentrations of secreted hormones and cytokines in the cell culture supernatant were quantified using commercial ELISA kits. Briefly, following the treatments, supernatants from each group were collected and centrifuged at 1000 × g for 20 minutes to remove cell debris. The levels of Estradiol (RuixinBio, RXJ106056H), LH (RuixinBio, RX106050H), FSH (RuixinBio, RX106046H), Testosterone (RuixinBio, JRX106316), TNF-α (RuixinBio, RX1600891C), and IL-6 (RuixinBio, RXQ96) were then determined. All assays were performed strictly in accordance with the manufacturer’s protocols. 2.9 Western blot To perform immunoblot analysis, total protein was harvested from KGN cells utilizing RIPA lysis buffer (Solarbio, R0020) supplemented with a protease inhibitor (PMSF, Sigma-Aldrich, P7626). Determination of the protein content within the lysates was accomplished via a BCA protein assay kit (Biosharp, BL521A). Identical quantities of protein from every sample were heat-denatured, resolved by 8%-12% SDS-PAGE, and thereafter electro-transferred onto PVDF membranes (Merck Millipore, IPVH00010). Non-specific binding sites on these membranes were blocked at ambient temperature for one hour using 5% non-fat milk dissolved in TBST. Following blocking, the membranes were probed overnight at 4 °C with the following primary antibodies: anti-PI3K (Bioss, BS-10657R, 1:800), anti-p-PI3K (CST, 17366, 1:800), anti-Akt (CST, 9279, 1:800), anti-p-Akt (CST, 4060, 1:1000), anti-PGR (Abcam, AB60954, 1:800), and anti-β-actin (Proteintech, 20536-1-AP, 1:5000). After washing, the membranes were incubated for 1 hour at room temperature with the appropriate HRP-conjugated secondary antibodies (1:10000, Proteintech). Finally, immunoreactive protein bands were visualized with an ECL detection system (Meilunbio, MA0186). Densitometric analysis was conducted using ImageJ, with β-actin serving as the internal loading control. Phosphorylation levels were expressed as the ratio of p-PI3K to total PI3K and p-Akt to total Akt, normalized to β-actin where appropriate. 2.10 RT-qPCR The initial step involved extracting total RNA from KGN cells with the TransZol Up Plus RNA Kit (TransGen Biotech, ER501-01). Following quantification, reverse transcription was conducted using TUAFS SuperMix (TransGen Biotech, AU341); this kit notably includes a procedure for genomic DNA (gDNA) elimination. This newly synthesized cDNA served as the template for quantitative RT-PCR analysis. The reactions were executed on a CFX Connect System (Bio-Rad) utilizing the MagicSYBR Mixture (CWBIO, CW3008). The cycling protocol was programmed for an initial 10-minute denaturation at 95°C, preceding 40 amplification cycles (10 s at 95°C, 30 s at 60°C, and 30 s at 72°C). All oligonucleotide primers, which are detailed in , were commercially produced by Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China). Calculation of relative mRNA abundance was achieved via the 2 −ΔΔCt method, wherein GAPDH served as the endogenous control for normalization. 2.11 Statistical analysis All quantitative data are expressed as the mean ± standard deviation (SD), derived from a minimum of three independent experiments. The statistical analyses were carried out using GraphPad Prism software (version 9.0, GraphPad Software, USA). Prior to analysis, data normality and homogeneity of variance were verified using the Shapiro-Wilk test and Levene’s test, respectively. A one-way Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test was applied for comparisons between multiple groups. A p-value less than 0.05 was set as the threshold for statistical significance. 3 Results 3.1 Network pharmacology analysis predicts key targets of GSW associated with PCOS-relevant pathways To elucidate the key therapeutic targets of GSW in treating PCOS, we first analyzed its serum-absorbed components ( ). 1477 potential drug targets for these components were predicted using the SwissTargetPrediction, TCMSP, and SymMap databases. This prediction was screened using pharmacokinetic parameters, requiring an OB of ≥ 30% and a DL score ≥ 0.18 ( ). To illustrate these interactions, a “drug-component-target” map was generated utilizing the Cytoscape software (version 3.7.2). The network included 399 nodes and 3122 edges, with diamond, rectangular, and circular nodes representing the drug, its components, and the targets, respectively. The top five active components, ranked by degree, were embelin, sesamin, nobiletin, dopamine, and histamine. Notably, embelin, sesamin, and nobiletin were associated with the highest number of potential targets, suggesting that these multi-target compounds may play a pivotal role in the therapeutic mechanism of GSW ( ). The network included 399 nodes and 3122 edges, with diamond, rectangular, and circular nodes representing the drug, its components, and the targets, respectively. The top five active components, ranked by degree, were embelin, sesamin, nobiletin, dopamine, and histamine. Notably, embelin, sesamin, and nobiletin were associated with the highest number of potential targets, suggesting that these multi-target compounds may play a pivotal role in the therapeutic mechanism of GSW ( ). To analyze the interplay among these potential targets, a PPI network was constructed for the 272 common targets by querying the STRING database (interaction score > 0.4). This analysis produced a network of 271 nodes and 6863 edges ( ). Hub genes were then obtained from this network by the CytoHubba plugin, which employed five distinct algorithms (MCC, MNC, Degree, EPC, and BottleNeck). A consensus analysis of the leading genes identified by all algorithms yielded four central hub nodes: IL-6, TNF, INS, and GAPDH ( ). GAPDH emerged as a hub node likely due to its central role in cellular metabolism and its extensive interactions in protein–protein interaction networks, rather than being interpreted as a specific therapeutic target. 3.2 Functional and pathway enrichment analysis of the common targets of GSW and PCOS To elucidate the biological roles and molecular cascades that GSW modulates relative to PCOS, GO and KEGG functional enrichment evaluations were conducted on the 272 shared targets, utilizing the DAVID platform. Applying a statistical cutoff of P < 0.05, the Gene Ontology annotation identified 3066 BP items, 113 CC items, and 261 MF items. Within the BP classification, these shared targets showed notable enrichment in functions including the inflammatory response, drug response, response to lipopolysaccharide, steroid metabolism, and the positive control of cell proliferation, suggesting that GSW’s therapeutic effects are closely related to the modulation of inflammation, hormone metabolism, and cell growth status. In the CC category, target proteins were predominantly localized to the extracellular space, plasma membrane, and cytosol, indicating that GSW’s targets are widely distributed, encompassing cell surface receptors, extracellular signaling molecules, and intracellular proteins. In the MF category, the targets were primarily associated with cytokine activity, enzyme binding, and steroid binding, confirming their involvement in complex protein-protein interactions and signal transduction ( ). The KEGG pathway enrichment evaluation identified 170 pathways showing significant enrichment (P < 0.05), with the leading ten being visualized in a bubble plot. These findings revealed that the common targets were significantly enriched in multiple cascades highly relevant to PCOS pathophysiology. Notably, the Lipid and atherosclerosis pathway was the most highly enriched, consistent with the dyslipidemia commonly associated with PCOS. Furthermore, the IL-17 and TNF signaling pathway were significantly enriched, directly indicating that inflammation is a key aspect of GSW’s mechanism of action. The PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, a critical intracellular hub whose dysfunction is directly linked to insulin resistance in PCOS, was also prominently identified. Other notable enriched pathways included the HIF-1 signaling pathway, Apoptosis, and MAPK signaling pathway ( ). Collectively, these enrichment analyses suggest that the core mechanism of GSW in treating PCOS involves its broad anti-inflammatory effects and the modulation of key signaling pathways, particularly the PI3K-Akt and TNF pathways, which are closely associated with inflammation, cell metabolism, and survival. 3.3 GSW-medicated serum ameliorates proliferation, apoptosis, and hormone secretion in the PCOS cell model To validate the therapeutic effects of GSW on PCOS, we treated the in vitro cell model with GSW-medicated serum. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that the induction of the PCOS model significantly increased the cellular apoptosis rate compared to the control group. Treatment with serum from GSW-administered rats, however, dose-dependently attenuated this pro-apoptotic effect ( ). Consistent with these findings, the CCK-8 assay demonstrated that the GSW-medicated serum significantly enhanced the viability of the PCOS model cells in a dose-dependent manner ( ). Furthermore, to elucidate the impact of GSW on hormone secretion, the levels of estradiol, LH, testosterone, and FSH were measured. These data indicated a significant hormonal imbalance in the model group compared to the control. Treatment with GSW-medicated serum led to a dose-dependent decrease in the secretion of estradiol, LH, and testosterone, while concurrently causing a dose-dependent increase in FSH secretion, suggesting that GSW-medicated serum partially restored the steroidogenic/hormone secretion profile in the granulosa cell PCOS-like model ( ). Notably, measurements of hormones/cytokines in the culture supernatant reflect in vitro outputs under the current experimental conditions and should not be extrapolated to systemic endocrine regulation in vivo . 3.4 GSW suppresses inflammatory responses and activates the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway in a PCOS cell model Based on the network pharmacology analysis, we investigated the effects of GSW-medicated serum on inflammation and the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway in PCOS model. Notably, measurements of hormones/cytokines in the culture supernatant reflect in vitro outputs under the current experimental conditions and should not be extrapolated to systemic endocrine regulation in vivo . 3.4 GSW suppresses inflammatory responses and activates the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway in a PCOS cell model Based on the network pharmacology analysis, we investigated the effects of GSW-medicated serum on inflammation and the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway in PCOS model. The results showed a potent anti-inflammatory effect that GSW-medicated serum treatment caused a dose-dependent reduction in both the protein secretion and mRNA expression levels of IL-6 and TNF-α when compared to the model group ( ). We then evaluated the impact on the PI3K/Akt signaling cascade. Western blot analysis indicated that GSW-medicated serum, in a dose-dependent manner, significantly increased the phosphorylation levels of both PI3K and Akt. We also assessed the expression of PGR, a critical protein for ovulation. Protein expression of PGR was significantly downregulated in the model group, but GSW-medicated serum treatment effectively restored its levels in a dose-dependent manner ( ). 3.5 GSW activates the PI3K/Akt pathway by suppressing TNF-α-mediated inhibition To further validate the relationship between TNF-α and the PI3K/Akt pathway during GSW treatment, a rescue experiment was conducted using recombinant human TNF-α to interfere with the therapeutic effects of GSW. Flow cytometry analysis revealed that the administration of TNF-α alone exacerbated apoptosis in the PCOS model cells. Critically, when cells were co-treated with GSW and TNF-α, the protective anti-apoptotic effect of GSW was significantly reversed ( ). Western blot analysis further delineated the molecular link between TNF-α and the PI3K/Akt pathway. The phosphorylation levels of PI3K and Akt were significantly downregulated in the model group compared to the control, and this suppression was further exacerbated by the addition of TNF-α. While GSW treatment markedly upregulated the phosphorylation of PI3K and Akt, this activated signaling effect was significantly attenuated by co-incubation with TNF-α ( ). The recombinant TNF-α rescue experiment was designed to specifically test the causal relationship between inflammatory suppression and PI3K/Akt activation, rather than to comprehensively map all upstream inflammatory mediators. Taken together, these results strongly suggest that the therapeutic activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway by GSW is dependent on its ability to suppress TNF-α, highlighting TNF-α as a critical therapeutic target of GSW in PCOS. 3.6 Embelin and nobiletin as key bioactive components of GSW exerting anti-PCOS effects To further identify the key bioactive components of GSW, we treated the PCOS model cells with the top five active ingredients predicted by network pharmacology: embelin, sesamin, nobiletin, dopamine, and histamine. These candidates were selected because they were not only predicted as top-ranking compounds by network pharmacology but were also confirmed to be present in the GSW-medicated serum via UPLC-MS/MS analysis. ELISA results revealed that embelin and nobiletin significantly reduced the secretion of TNF-α, while sesamin showed a modest inhibitory effect. In contrast, dopamine had no significant effect, and histamine slightly increased TNF-α secretion ( ). Based on these findings, the effects of embelin and nobiletin were investigated further. Western blot analysis demonstrated that both embelin, as well as nobiletin, stimulated the phosphorylation of both PI3K and Akt. This effect was observed in a dose-dependent fashion, as high concentrations yielded a more potent response than low concentrations. Notably, the combined application of low-dose embelin and low-dose nobiletin resulted in a significantly more potent activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway compared to the effect of either compound at low dose level. These results suggest that embelin and nobiletin are key components responsible for the anti-PCOS action of GSW and that they function cooperatively to exert an enhanced effect, consistent with the multi-component therapeutic theory of TCM ( ). 4 Discussion This study systematically elucidates the molecular mechanisms by which GSW ameliorates PCOS in vitro , by integrating network pharmacology analysis with a series of cellular experiments. Our findings demonstrate that GSW, partly through its active components such as embelin and nobiletin, significantly suppresses TNF-α-mediated inflammatory responses, thereby restoring the impaired PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. This effect enhances proliferation in the PCOS model, suppresses cellular apoptosis, and normalizes the dysregulated production of sex hormones. A persistent condition of low-grade inflammation represents a critical factor in the pathophysiology of PCOS, contributing to insulin resistance, hyperandrogenism, and ovarian dysfunction ( – ). It is well-documented that individuals with PCOS, encompassing both lean and obese phenotypes, frequently exhibit markedly increased concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α. These cytokines are strongly linked to insulin resistance, hyperandrogenism, and oxidative stress ( – ). Our findings affirm that GSW-medicated serum significantly diminishes not only the protein secretion but also the mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically

PCOS model, suppresses cellular apoptosis, and normalizes the dysregulated production of sex hormones. A persistent condition of low-grade inflammation represents a critical factor in the pathophysiology of PCOS, contributing to insulin resistance, hyperandrogenism, and ovarian dysfunction ( – ). It is well-documented that individuals with PCOS, encompassing both lean and obese phenotypes, frequently exhibit markedly increased concentrations of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α. These cytokines are strongly linked to insulin resistance, hyperandrogenism, and oxidative stress ( – ). Our findings affirm that GSW-medicated serum significantly diminishes not only the protein secretion but also the mRNA expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically TNF-α and IL-6, in a PCOS cellular model. This indicates that GSW regulates inflammation primarily at the transcriptional level, thereby suppressing the de novo synthesis and subsequent release of these cytokines, rather than merely blocking their secretion. Inhibiting these core inflammatory mediators is a crucial strategy for intervening in the progression of PCOS. This finding is consistent with numerous studies on the treatment of PCOS or related inflammatory conditions with TCM. For instance, the YJKL formula was predicted via network pharmacology to target TNF-α in PCOS treatment ( ), while the Cuscutae Semen-Salviae Miltiorrhizae formula was shown to ameliorate PCOS by modulating inflammatory factors such as IL-6 and TNF-α ( ). Furthermore, TCM formulas like Liu Shen Wan and Jin Gui Shen Qi Wan have been reported to exert anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting pro-inflammatory cytokines ( , ). By revealing the anti-inflammatory efficacy of GSW, our study positions it as a potential therapeutic agent for PCOS that acts through an inflammation-centric mechanism, similar to these previously reported TCM formulas. Moreover, therapeutic strategies targeting TNF-α have shown positive outcomes in PCOS animal models; for example, TNF-α inhibitor Etanercept effectively mitigated symptoms and metabolic dysfunction in letrozole-induced PCOS rats, further supporting the importance of anti-inflammatory therapy in PCOS ( ). Our findings emphasize that granulosa cells are active participants in this inflammatory landscape. While conventional views focus on systemic immune cell infiltration, our data suggest that GCs themselves, under metabolic stress induced by insulin and dexamethasone, become a significant source of TNF-α and IL-6. This autonomous cytokine production may contribute to a local inflammatory milieu that impairs PI3K/Akt-mediated insulin signaling and steroidogenesis, thereby linking metabolic stress to reproductive dysfunction. Our study establishes a link demonstrating that the activation of the PI3K/Akt pathway by GSW is dependent on its inhibition of TNF-α. In the pathogenesis of PCOS, excessive levels of TNF-α are considered a key factor causing insulin resistance and ovarian dysfunction, as it can directly or indirectly suppress the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway ( , ). The PI3K/Akt pathway is not only implicated in the formation of PCOS but can also be modulated by natural products. For example, Rhei Radix Et Rhizome was found to improve ovarian morphology and hormone levels in PCOS rats by regulating the PI3K/Akt pathway ( ). Berberine has also been shown to ameliorate insulin resistance and apoptosis in PCOS rats via the same pathway ( ). Furthermore, various interventions, including melatonin and luteolin, have been reported to alleviate PCOS symptoms by activating PI3K/Akt signaling ( , ). These studies collectively confirmed the crucial role of the PI3K/Akt pathway in the treatment of PCOS. However, GSW is different from single-target drugs or other generic formulations. These findings support a model in which GSW attenuates TNF-α–driven inflammatory signaling while concomitantly restoring PI3K/Akt activity. This TNF-α/PI3K/Akt-centered axis provides a parsimonious mechanistic framework for interpreting the observed cellular phenotypes. In this study, the key active components embelin and nobiletin were shown to mimic the anti-inflammatory and pathway-activating effects of GSW, with their combined application demonstrating an enhanced effect. Embelin is recognized for its anti-inflammatory capabilities. In parallel, nobiletin, which is a flavonoid, is reported in various studies to possess promising anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, and insulin-sensitizing functions. This aligns with findings for other related compounds, such as quercetin. Quercetin is known to suppress inflammation by blocking the TLR/NF-κB pathway, which in turn reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α and IL-6), and simultaneously stimulates the PI3K/Akt signaling cascade ( , ). The combined action of multi-component, multi-target therapy is a unique advantage of TCM formulas, offering a more comprehensive and durable therapeutic effect. For instance, research on Si Shen Wan has revealed its multi-component enhanced pharmacokinetic effects, indicating that the combined action of multiple active ingredients is necessary for optimal efficacy ( ). The combined anti-inflammatory and PI3K/Akt-activating effects of embelin and nobiletin in GSW provide a novel direction for developing natural product-based therapies for PCOS. Despite the significant progress made, this study has certain limitations. First, the present work is primarily based on an in vitro granulosa cell model. While this system allows mechanistic dissection of cytokine-driven signaling events, it does not recapitulate the complex systemic endocrine–metabolic–immune interactions that characterize PCOS in vivo . Second, a

Si Shen Wan has revealed its multi-component enhanced pharmacokinetic effects, indicating that the combined action of multiple active ingredients is necessary for optimal efficacy ( ). The combined anti-inflammatory and PI3K/Akt-activating effects of embelin and nobiletin in GSW provide a novel direction for developing natural product-based therapies for PCOS. Despite the significant progress made, this study has certain limitations. First, the present work is primarily based on an in vitro granulosa cell model. While this system allows mechanistic dissection of cytokine-driven signaling events, it does not recapitulate the complex systemic endocrine–metabolic–immune interactions that characterize PCOS in vivo . Second, a rat medicated serum approach was employed to reflect in vivo absorption and metabolic transformation of the herbal formula. Although this method is widely used in traditional Chinese medicine research, cross-species differences and the heat-inactivation process may influence the stability and composition of bioactive metabolites. Consequently, the observed effects are more likely to reflect conserved inflammatory and metabolic signaling mechanisms rather than species-specific responses. Third, the network pharmacology analysis applied stringent screening criteria (OB ≥ 30% and DL ≥ 0.18), which favor compounds with predicted drug-like properties. This strategy may inadvertently exclude certain bioactive constituents with lower predicted bioavailability that could nonetheless contribute to the therapeutic effects of GSW. Fourth, KGN cells are a tumor-derived granulosa cell line and may not fully mirror the biological behavior of primary human granulosa cells. Therefore, caution is warranted when extrapolating these findings to physiological ovarian function. Fifth, this study focused on TNF-α-centered inflammatory signaling within granulosa cells and did not investigate immune cell–derived inflammatory components, such as macrophage or T-cell involvement, nor broader cytokine networks that may participate in PCOS pathogenesis. Finally, while the key roles of embelin and nobiletin were validated, GSW is a complex formula containing numerous other active components. Whether other constituents also contribute synergistically to the amelioration of PCOS, and the complexity of their interactions warrants further investigation. Moving forward, rigorous clinical trials combined with mechanistic validation, similar to recent comprehensive studies on other TCM formulae ( ), are necessary to confirm the therapeutic efficacy of GSW and its active components in PCOS patients. In conclusion, this study provides evidence that GSW ameliorates the pathological state of PCOS in vitro by inhibiting TNF-α-mediated inflammation, thereby restoring the impaired PI3K/Akt signaling pathway. These findings not only provide a solid modern pharmacological basis for the use of GSW in treating PCOS but also highlight the multi-target, holistic advantages of TCM in managing complex diseases. Although these findings provide mechanistic insight into the anti-inflammatory effects of GSW at the cellular level, they should not be interpreted as direct evidence of clinical efficacy. In vivo validation and clinical studies are required before translational conclusions can be drawn. This work supports further in vivo and clinical investigation of GSW and its active components for PCOS.

documents.title: Vaginal Birth After Cesarean

chunks.content: Introduction Cesarean section (C/S) rates have increased around the world within the last 30 years [ ]. The World Health Organization (WHO) stated that 21% of births globally occur with cesarean sections, and the cesarean birth rates are higher than vaginal birth rates in the Dominican Republic, Brazil, Cyprus, Egypt and Türkiye [ ]. According to OECD Health Data for 2021, the cesarean birth rate in Türkiye was 60.1%, first place among all countries, while the Health Statistics Yearbook for 2023 reported a cesarean rate of 64.2% in Türkiye [ , ]. The terms “natural birth” and “normal vaginal birth” have sociolinguistic implications that portray vaginal delivery as the standard or ideal method of childbirth. This reinforces the perception that C-sections are less natural or inferior [ , ]. Though birth is a physiological event, in some situations it is not possible for birth to occur through the vaginal route, or this involves life-threatening risks to the mother and baby. In these medical situations, C/S is life-saving. Cesarean section may be performed for various medically indicated reasons, including fetal indications (non-reassuring fetal heart rate patterns, labor dystocia), maternal obstetric indications (malpresentation, cephalopelvic disproportion, placenta previa, placental abruption), and maternal medical indications (preeclampsia, eclampsia, active genital infections, previous uterine surgery such as classical C/S or myomectomy) [ ]. However, it is important to note that birth may also occur with elective C/S without any medical necessity. Cases accepted as maternal choice may include women with a history of trauma, sexual abuse, or anxiety related to previous pregnancy loss [ , ]. Scientific sources, health professionals and media defend normal birth while presenting cesarean section as unacceptable, thus creating a prejudice against cesarean section in society. When studies aiming to measure the risks or benefits of C/S are presented to society poorly against this cultural background, women may experience feelings of guilt and shame related to C/S birth [ , ]. In the context of Turkish culture, certain cultural beliefs have been identified that idealize vaginal birth. These beliefs include the notion that childbirth facilitates the expulsion of illnesses and that experiencing labor pain is a prerequisite for the development of a strong maternal identity. Within this cultural framework, women who give birth via cesarean section may be perceived as lacking the “natural” transition into motherhood. Assumptions are made that they will struggle to bond with their babies or that they will have difficulty “standing up immediately” and fulfilling maternal roles [ , ]. These beliefs have the potential to engender implicit biases against women who deliver by cesarean section. Information about the risks and outcomes of cesarean birth is often communicated inadequately within society, and this, together with prevailing prejudices may exacerbate postpartum mental health difficulties by increasing feelings of shame, inadequacy, or failure among women regarding the mode of delivery. In the literature, it has been shown that even women who give birth by cesarean section may recommend vaginal birth to others, reflecting the strong societal discourse that positions vaginal birth as superior in terms of breastfeeding, bonding, and maternal functionality [ , ]. Such beliefs may cause women who deliver by cesarean to feel deficient or less capable as mothers [ , , ]. On a global scale, the reasons for rising C/S rates and the strategies employed to reduce them are subjects of ongoing investigation [ ]. However, the present study was motivated by the reality that in Türkiye, nearly one in two women has given birth by C/S. Despite the rising incidence of C/S, prevailing societal attitudes toward C/S birth remain unfavorable, underscoring the necessity for a comprehensive examination of how these attitudes influence perceptions of women who prefer C/S. It is imperative to acknowledge the significance of endeavors aimed at reducing C/S rates, both within the confines of Türkiye and on a global scale. Nevertheless, it is equally critical to ensure that women who undergo cesarean birth are socially accepted and not subjected to stigma or judgment. Although a scale measuring women’s personal attitudes toward cesarean birth has previously been developed in Türkiye [ ], there is no instrument designed to capture the broader society’s views toward C/S in a comprehensive manner. To the best of our knowledge, only one study has been conducted on this topic internationally. The present study was constrained to the local cultural context of a specific country and focused exclusively on men’s perspectives [ ]. In Türkiye, where cultural expectations surrounding childbirth are particularly pronounced, it is essential to identify and quantify the negative societal attitudes directed towards women who deliver by C/S. Materials and methods Study design The methodological research was carried out in 3 stages (1). developing the item pool (2), content validity and expert opinion, and (3) psychometric properties.
