chunks.content: Introduction Although hemorrhoid disease is prevalent, the exact frequency of hemorrhoids remains elusive, because symptoms of anorectal pain are frequently associated with this condition [ ]. A comprehensive cross-sectional study performed in the United States revealed that the self-reported incidence of symptomatic hemorrhoids stood at 4.4% [ ]. Furthermore, hemorrhoids were detected in about 39% of colonoscopies according to colonoscopy data [ ]. Annually, hemorrhoids account for approximately 2.5 million outpatient visits in the United States [ ]. Surgery is the most effective treatment for grade III or IV hemorrhoids [ ]. The procedure for prolapse and hemorrhoids (PPH), involving the removal of a circular ring of mucosal tissue above the dentate line, has been proven to improve short-term outcomes, particularly by reducing the severity of postoperative pain. PPH possesses the advantages of reduced operation time and diminished postoperative discomfort compared with traditional excisional hemorrhoidectomy, facilitating a faster resumption of daily activities and decreased length of hospitalization [ ]. However, some patients may experience severe pain, which is commonly described as"passing bits of broken glass,"especially during defecation. This pain is a significant factor in surgery refusal, as it leads to negative psychological effects, limited mobility, decreased self-care ability, and reduced recovery quality. Therefore, effective postoperative pain management is essential to address these concerns. Current clinical practice guidelines recommend multimodal analgesia for patients undergoing anorectal surgery, incorporating local anesthetic infiltration, systemic nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), and opioids [ ]. Although opioids are frequently utilized for postoperative pain management in anorectal surgery, their usage is often limited by side effects, such as nausea, constipation, and respiratory depression [ ]. The pudendal neurovascular bundle is located between the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments. Pudendal nerve block (PNB ) has been widely utilized in gynecological and penile surgeries; however, strong evidence supporting its use in anal surgeries, particularly for postoperative analgesia following hemorrhoidectomy, remains limited [ ]. The aim of this prospective, randomized, double-blinded study was to evaluate the postoperative analgesic efficacy of ultrasound-guided PNB compared to local infiltration analgesia in adults undergoing PPH. The study concentrated on outcomes, such as the visual analog scale (VAS), sphincter spasm, total analgesic consumption, complications, recovery within 48 h postoperatively, and patient satisfaction. Methods Study design and registration This prospective, randomized, double-blind, controlled trial received ethical approval from the Ethics Committee of Harbin Medical University (Harbin, China; Approval No. HMUIRB201500013) and was registered with the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry (Registration No. ChiCTR-IPR-15006427; Link: https://www.chictr.org.cn/showproj.html?proj=11023 ). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study included patients undergoing stapled hemorrhoidopexy under spinal anesthesia for Grade III or IV hemorrhoids from January 2015 to October 2015. Exclusion criteria were summarized as follows: patient’s age under 18 years, bleeding disorders, coagulopathy, chronic liver or kidney failure, allergy to local anesthetics, infection at the injection site, spinal anomalies, alcohol or analgesic dependence, and chronic pain. Participants were randomized in a 1:1 ratio to either the ultrasound-guided PNB (PNB group) or local anesthetic infiltration (LAI group) using a sealed envelope technique with computer-generated random numbers. All surgical procedures are performed by the same trained physician. Intervention Patients in the PNB group received 10 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine for each side, totaling 20 ml for bilateral PNB under ultrasound guidance, while those in the LAI group received 20 ml of 0.5% ropivacaine injected into the anal sphincter at the end of the surgery. The PNB was administered by an anesthesiologist, and the LAI was administered by a surgeon who was not involved in patient management. In the LAI group, after completion of the surgical procedure and under strict aseptic conditions, a total of 20 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine was administered into the anal sphincter region. Local infiltration was performed at the 3, 6, and 9 o’clock positions while the patient was in the lithotomy position. The injection site was approximately 1–2 cm from the anal verge, and the needle was inserted perpendicular to the skin surface and directed laterally toward the external anal sphincter. At each point, approximately 5–6 mL of anesthetic was administered, and aspiration was performed simultaneously to avoid intravascular injection. This technique was used to achieve full relaxation of the anal sphincter, facilitating surgical manipulation and providing postoperative analgesia. If additional incision-based pain was anticipated, subcutaneous infiltration of the anesthetic at the incision site was also performed to further enhance pain control. Prior to the PNB, strict aseptic preparation of both the skin and the ultrasound probe was carried out to minimize the risk of infection. Patients were positioned in the prone position to optimize access for the ultrasound examination of the gluteal region. Following the guidelines from Kovacs’s [ ] ultrasonographic investigation of the pudendal nerve, the present study employed a transverse plane to locate the pudendal nerve (PN) and the internal pudendal artery (IPA). This plane is typically

additional incision-based pain was anticipated, subcutaneous infiltration of the anesthetic at the incision site was also performed to further enhance pain control. Prior to the PNB, strict aseptic preparation of both the skin and the ultrasound probe was carried out to minimize the risk of infection. Patients were positioned in the prone position to optimize access for the ultrasound examination of the gluteal region. Following the guidelines from Kovacs’s [ ] ultrasonographic investigation of the pudendal nerve, the present study employed a transverse plane to locate the pudendal nerve (PN) and the internal pudendal artery (IPA). This plane is typically aligned with a line connecting the posterior superior iliac spine to the greater trochanter, providing a comprehensive view of the pertinent anatomical landmarks. The ultrasound probe was placed on the ischial tuberosity, which appeared as a hyperechoic line with a sound shadow in the ultrasound image. By moving the probe perpendicularly to the transverse plane in a cephalic direction, the inferior pudendal artery (IPA) was visualized as it traveled sagittally between the ischial spine (IS) and the space formed by the sacrotuberous ligament (STL) and the sacrospinous ligament (SSL). The location of the IPA was reconfirmed using color Doppler imaging (Fig. A). Next, a 20 G, 10 cm ultrasound-guided needle was inserted toward the IPA from the medial aspect of the probe (Fig. B, C). A characteristic ‘click’ sensation was typically felt as the needle passed through the STL. Afterward, 10 mL of ropivacaine was injected around the IPA, forming a hypoechoic collection as the anesthetic spread into the common connective tissue space between the two ligaments (Fig. D). This ultrasound-guided puncture procedure was performed by experienced anesthesiologists to ensure both accuracy and patient safety. All procedures were conducted under sterile conditions to prevent any potential infections. Primary and secondary endpoints The primary endpoint was postoperative pain assessed by the VAS within 48 h postoperatively. Secondary endpoints included time to the first request for analgesia, the usage of tramadol for rescue analgesia (a single intravenous injection of tramadol 100 mg was used when VAS > 4), postoperative complications (nausea, vomiting, urinary retention, or readmission due to severe pain), sphincter spasms, and the quality of recovery-15 (QoR-15) scores at 24 h, 48 h, and 4 weeks postoperatively. Further follow-up was conducted via telephone at 4 weeks postoperatively to assess overall satisfaction. Patients were specifically asked whether they would choose the same type of postoperative analgesia for a future procedure and whether they would recommend it to others undergoing similar surgery. Responses were recorded as either “yes” or “no.” Satisfaction was rated on a scale of 1 to 3, with 1 indicating “dissatisfied,” 2 “partially satisfied,” and 3 “satisfied.” To ensure blinding, all follow-ups and data collection were conducted by a different anesthesiologist who was unfamiliar with the group assignments. Preoperative preparation and surgical procedure Preoperatively, patients were required to fast and undergo bowel preparation. Spinal anesthesia was administered using 0.5% bupivacaine, while the patient was in the lateral position. The surgical procedure involved inserting a specially designed circular stapler into the rectum, excising the lower part of the rectal mucosa and submucosa, repositioning the anal sphincter, and preserving mucosal blood supply to prevent contraction due to hemorrhoidal arterial branch disruption. At the end of the surgery, vaseline gauze was gently placed in the anal canal, and a urinary catheter was inserted. Postoperative care Postoperative management included bed rest, fasting for 12 h postoperatively, prophylactic antibiotics to prevent infection, and intravenous administration of 100 mg flurbiprofen every 12 h for analgesia. Tramadol was administered as rescue analgesia for patients with VAS scores > 4. Additionally, 10 mg of metoclopramide was prescribed to prevent postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV). Sample size The sample size was determined based on the mean values of two independent groups on the VAS at 24 h [ – ]. A minimum of 39 patients per group was required, assuming a two-sided α of 0.05 and a power of 80% (1-β = 0.2), with a 1:1 allocation ratio and an anticipated dropout rate of approximately 10%. Statistical analysis Participants’ baseline characteristics were described using descriptive statistics. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), including age, height, weight, body mass index (BMI), and operation time. Categorical variables were presented as number (percentage). Group differences for continuous variables were analyzed using t-test, while Chi-square test was used for categorical variables. Repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed to evaluate the influences of the two analgesic methods on postoperative VAS pain scores and QoR satisfaction scores at different time points. Data analysis was performed using SAS statistical software (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Participants’ demographic and baseline characteristics A total of 78 patients

Group differences for continuous variables were analyzed using t-test, while Chi-square test was used for categorical variables. Repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was employed to evaluate the influences of the two analgesic methods on postoperative VAS pain scores and QoR satisfaction scores at different time points. Data analysis was performed using SAS statistical software (SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC, USA). All statistical tests were two-sided, and P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Participants’ demographic and baseline characteristics A total of 78 patients were initially randomized into two groups, involving 39 patients in each group. Attrition occurred with one patient from the PNB group and one from the LAI group declined to participate after randomization. Additionally, 2 patients were withdrawn from the PNB group due to early discharge for personal reasons, and 3 from the LAI group due to surgery cancellation because of fever (n = 1) and conversion to general anesthesia due to spinal abnormalities or anxiety (n = 2). Thus, 71 patients were included in the intention-to-treat analysis (Fig. ). There were no significant differences between the groups regarding sex, age, weight, height, BMI, and operation time (Table ). Primary outcomes Pain scores, assessed using the VAS at rest, are depicted in Fig. and Table . At 6, 12, and 18 h postoperatively, pain scores were significantly lower in the PNB group compared with the LAI group (all P < 0.01). However, no significant differences were identified between the two groups at 24 or 48 h postoperatively. Secondary outcomes The need for supplemental analgesia with tramadol was significantly less in the PNB group (5/36) compared with the LAI group (12/35) (Table ; P < 0.05). The incidence of PONV was similar between the PNB group (16.67%) and the LAI group (17.14%) (Table ). There were no cases of patient readmission due to severe pain in either group ( P > 0.05). The first onset of pain was significantly delayed in the PNB group (13.83 ± 11.21 h) compared with the LAI group (6.94 ± 2.88 h) ( P < 0.001; Table ). Additionally, the incidence of anal sphincter spasm was significantly lower in the PNB group (5/36) compared with the LAI group (12/35) ( P < 0.04; Table ). QoR-15 scores at 24 h postoperatively were significantly higher in the PNB group (119.11 ± 5.87) than those in the LAI group (112.03 ± 7.04) (Table ; P < 0.05), although no significant differences were found at 48 h (127.94 ± 4.25 vs. 127.03 ± 4.06) (Table ). Patient satisfaction and recommendations A significantly higher proportion of patients in the PNB group (28/36) expressed satisfaction with the pain management compared with the LAI group (22/35), while none in the PNB group were dissatisfied, compared with the LAI group (1/35) (all P < 0.05; Table ). Furthermore, a higher proportion of patients in the PNB group (30/36) were willing to recommend their pain management approach compared with those in the LAI group (26/35) ( P < 0.05; Table ). Discussion This is the first prospective, randomized, double-blinded study to evaluate the effectiveness of ultrasound-guided PNB for postoperative pain management in patients undergoing PPH. While several clinical trials [ , ] and corresponding meta-analyses [ , , ] consistently demonstrated that PNB effectively controls postoperative pain following hemorrhoid surgery, accompanying by advantages, such as decreased analgesic use, fewer postoperative complications, and shorter hospital stays. The specific types of hemorrhoid surgeries examined in these studies are either unspecified or involve procedures other than PPH. To date, there has been no study specifically evaluating the effectiveness of PNB in managing postoperative pain after PPH surgery. The findings of the present study indicated that PNB provided superior postoperative analgesia, prolonged pain relief, reduced the use of tramadol, and enhanced overall patient satisfaction compared with LAI among patients undergoing PPH. The efficacy of the randomization was validated by the comparable baseline demographics and operation time between the two groups, indicating that differences found in outcomes were attributable to the interventions rather than underlying patient characteristics. Hemorrhoids, particularly in advanced stages (grade III and IV), mainly necessitate surgical intervention, and PPH is a frequently used and effective procedure to reduce postoperative pain and improve recovery [ ]. Despite the advancements, PPH is associated with remarkable postoperative pain, with the VAS scores exceeding 4 in up to 40% of cases within the first 24–48 h following surgery [ , ]. The pudendal neurovascular bundle, which runs between the STL and SSL, mainly innervates the vulva and the perineum. It consists of the anterior branch of S2-4 nerve, which exits the pelvis from the greater foramen of the sciatic bone, goes around the sacrospinous ligament, enters the pelvis through the sciatic

and PPH is a frequently used and effective procedure to reduce postoperative pain and improve recovery [ ]. Despite the advancements, PPH is associated with remarkable postoperative pain, with the VAS scores exceeding 4 in up to 40% of cases within the first 24–48 h following surgery [ , ]. The pudendal neurovascular bundle, which runs between the STL and SSL, mainly innervates the vulva and the perineum. It consists of the anterior branch of S2-4 nerve, which exits the pelvis from the greater foramen of the sciatic bone, goes around the sacrospinous ligament, enters the pelvis through the sciatic foramen and reaches the ischiorectal fossa, and travels to the lower medial part of the sciatic tubercle. It is divided into three branches, namely, the inferior anal nerve, the dorsal clitoris nerve and the perineal nerve, which innervate the skin around the anus, the anal extensor muscle and the labia, respectively. PNB is to reduce the sensitivity of perianal cells to pain and play an analgesic role by blocking the afferent impulse of pudendal nerve pathway [ ]. Ultrasound guidance enables accurate localization of this bundle, helping to avoid accidental vessel injection and potential adverse effects associated with intrathecal morphine administration [ , ]. The present study utilized ultrasonographic landmarks, including the internal pudendal artery (IPA) and ischial spine (IS), to enhance the accuracy of the nerve block. In addition, the anatomical structure of the target area can be displayed in real time, which is convenient for the anesthesiologist to grasp the injection position and the dispersion of local anesthesia drugs in real time, achieve the ideal analgesic effect. This precise methodology resulted in significantly lower VAS scores during the first 18 h post-surgery and reduced analgesic requirements in the PNB group compared with the LAI group. The extended pain-free period observed in the PNB group confirmed the effectiveness of peripheral nerve block in achieving a more durable analgesic effect. This result is consistent with the current literature, supporting the advantages of peripheral nerve blocks for postoperative pain management [ , , ]. Postoperative quality of life is a clinically significant outcome, and the improvement in postoperative quality of life has not been previously reported. The findings indicated that the QoR-15 scores were notably higher in the PNB group at 24 h postoperatively, suggesting an enhanced overall recovery experience. The success of PNB can be influenced by anatomical variability [ ]. In the present study, a case of unintended sciatic nerve blockage was identified, which could be attributed to proximity to the sciatic nerves during the block performed at the infrapiriformis foramen. This incident highlights the importance of understanding anatomical variations, including the presence of multiple pudendal nerve trunks and their relationships with surrounding structures. The findings of this study also emphasize the importance of patient-centered care. The high rates of patient satisfaction and willingness to recommend the PNB technique observed in this study underscore the potential of PNB to improve perioperative management and patient experiences. The comprehensive assessment encompasses not only the physical aspects, but also the psychological and emotional recovery, both of which are critical components of a successful postoperative recovery. While this study provided compelling evidence supporting the use of ultrasound-guided PNB in PPH, it was conducted in a single medical center with a relatively small sample size, and no optimal dose of local anesthetic was explored. Additional multicenter, large-scale trials are needed to validate the findings and refine the technique to maximize its benefits. These findings are also reported for the first time. Conclusion In conclusion, ultrasound-guided PNB presents a viable and effective alternative to traditional local anesthetic infiltration for managing postoperative pain in PPH. It provides significant benefits in terms of pain relief, reduced need for additional analgesics, and enhanced recovery quality, thereby supporting its broader adoption in clinical practice.

chunks.content: Introduction Cervical cancer constitutes a public health problem worldwide, representing the fourth most common cancer type and one of the leading causes of cancer-related deaths in women [ ]. Cervical cancer typically develops through a long precancerous phase represented by cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN). While CIN 1 is considered a low-grade lesion (LSIL) without a precursor potential, CIN2 and CIN 3 are regarded as high-grade lesions related to a higher risk for progression to cancer [ – ]. Some studies have consistently shown that most CIN2 lesions regress spontaneously, particularly in women younger than 30. A meta-analysis and recent cohort studies advocate conservative management in selected cases of CIN2, emphasizing personalized care that avoids overtreatment while ensuring oncologic safety [ – ]. This is especially relevant because excisional treatment has been linked to adverse obstetric outcomes [ – ]. Therefore, avoiding unnecessary treatment is particularly important in reproductive-aged women. This discussion is particularly relevant in Brazil and other countries, where guidelines recommend excision for CIN2 based only on patients’ age [ ], while maternal age is increasing [ ]. The proportion of mothers aged 30 years or older increased from 23.7% in 2000 [ ] to 37.7% of live births in 2020 in Brazil [ ]. CIN2 is a heterogeneous diagnosis that encompasses both transient HPV-related changes and true precursor lesions. Moreover, the diagnosis of CIN2 is characterized by significant interobserver variability [ – ]. To address this issue, the Lower Anogenital Squamous Terminology (LAST) guidelines recommend using p16 immunohistochemistry to refine CIN2 diagnoses, stratifying lesions into high-grade or low-grade based on p16 staining patterns. This distinction has prognostic implications, as p16-positive CIN2 lesions may be less likely to regress [ ]. p16 is a tumor suppressor protein that is consistently overexpressed in high-risk HPV (hr-HPV) associated lesions, correlating with diagnostic reproducibility, diagnostic accuracy, and disease progression [ – ]. Some studies have demonstrated its usefulness in managing CIN2 due to its high negative predictive value; however, p16 positivity alone is not sufficient to indicate excisional treatment [ , ]. Ki-67 is a nuclear proliferation marker that has also been associated with CIN grade and lesion progression [ , ]. However, its prognostic value in guiding treatment versus surveillance remains controversial [ ]. There is no consensus on the cutoff point for positive Ki-67 expression, but the 50% cutoff has been associated with CIN 3 or carcinoma in previous studies [ , ]. Therefore, this study aimed to describe the clinical outcomes and time-to-event patterns of conservatively managed, biopsy-confirmed CIN2 cases in a Brazilian public healthcare setting and to explore whether selected baseline characteristics—p16, Ki-67, age, and referral cytology—were associated with lesion regression. Materials and methods Study design and setting This was a bidirectional cohort study, including both retrospectively identified and prospectively enrolled patients, at a reference center for cervical uterine pathology and colposcopy within the Brazilian Unified Health System (SUS) in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Cases were identified from the institutional database (2006–2018) and from consecutive referrals to the colposcopy clinic during the study period (2018–2022). All patients were referred to colposcopy due to abnormal cervical cytology originating from primary care units within the same geographic region. Diagnostic criteria, colposcopy procedures, immunohistochemical protocols, histopathological review, and outcome definitions remained unchanged throughout the study period, ensuring consistency in data collection and clinical management. Cohort definition Given that all patients originated from the same source population and were investigated, managed, reviewed, and followed using identical clinical and pathological protocols, all cases were analyzed as a single cohort. Sample size All cases that met the inclusion/exclusion criteria during the study period determined the sample size. Although a larger sample size had been initially planned, the final cohort reflects the cases available for analysis within the predefined study period. Inclusion criteria Patients with confirmed biopsy diagnosis of CIN2 on H&E, independently reviewed by two pathologists, who had not undergone treatment at the time of diagnosis, presented with a fully visible SCJ on colposcopy (transformation zones types 1 or 2), and had no previous history of pre-invasive or invasive cervical disease. Exclusion criteria Patients living with Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) or other immunodeficiency conditions, pregnant women, cases immediately treated, cases in which the cervical biopsy was considered excisional (defined as cases in which the entire lesion was intentionally removed during the procedure), cases of biopsy failure were excluded from the study (defined as cases where a more severe diagnosis was made at the immediately subsequent visit), and cases with no follow-up proposed (defined as cases in which immediate treatment was proposed but patient did not return for treatment). Follow-up All women included in this study were prospectively followed according to a standardized conservative management protocol, including semiannual cytology and colposcopy, until treatment or discharge from follow-up. Excisional treatment was undertaken if persistent lesions were

biopsy was considered excisional (defined as cases in which the entire lesion was intentionally removed during the procedure), cases of biopsy failure were excluded from the study (defined as cases where a more severe diagnosis was made at the immediately subsequent visit), and cases with no follow-up proposed (defined as cases in which immediate treatment was proposed but patient did not return for treatment). Follow-up All women included in this study were prospectively followed according to a standardized conservative management protocol, including semiannual cytology and colposcopy, until treatment or discharge from follow-up. Excisional treatment was undertaken if persistent lesions were evident after 24 months of follow-up or if progression occurred at any point during the observation period. Clinical follow-up procedures and outcomes assessment were identical for all women, regardless of the period of inclusion. For women enrolled earlier in the study period (before July 2018), baseline and follow-up information were retrieved from medical records; for those enrolled later (from July 2018), the data were collected prospectively during scheduled visits. Importantly, in both situations, the decision to treat or not was based on cytological and colposcopic evaluation, following the same institutional protocol. Women who, despite not presenting with cytological or colposcopic evidence of progression, opted for treatment during follow-up were also included and contributed to the total follow-up time. This study was concluded on May 31, 2024. Loss to follow-up was defined as the absence of, or incomplete, follow-up examination after the initial biopsy, preventing a proper determination of their outcomes. These losses were attributed to social factors and were unrelated to the outcomes. Follow-up time For each participant, follow-up began on the date of the diagnostic (index) biopsy, which confirmed CIN2. Participants were followed until the earliest of: (1) date of excisional treatment, (2) date of histologically confirmed progression (CIN3 or carcinoma), (3) date of last clinical contact (right-censoring), (4) date of first documented regression (histological regression to ≤CIN1 or cytology/colposcopy criteria consistent with regression as defined ahead. In this case, the date of the first documented regression was used to define the time to regression. However, patients continued to be monitored for at least 2 years of follow-up. If evidence of persistence or progression was identified during this period, the patient was reclassified as demonstrating no regression, and the date on which progression or persistence was observed was recorded for analysis purposes. Event dates correspond to the date of diagnostic confirmation (histology or cytology/colposcopy). Because events were ascertained at scheduled semiannual visits, exact times of biological change may fall between visits. Clinical outcomes This analysis classified outcomes as regression, persistence, or progression at the end of the patient’s follow-up period, regardless of whether this was due to excisional treatment, patient dropout, discharge, or study period termination. Regression cases were those with histological results of ≤CIN 1 in the specimen after the initial biopsy or, in the absence of histological data, cytological examinations classified as a normal, inflammatory, low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (LSIL) or atypical squamous cells of undetermined significance (ASC-US), and colposcopy with no or minor abnormal findings [ ]. Complete regression was defined as the return of all exams performed during follow-up to normal (histopathological or cytological report negative for malignancy or intraepithelial lesion, colposcopy with no abnormal findings, and fully visible SCJ). Persistence was defined as a histologic diagnosis of CIN2 during follow-up. The diagnosis of CIN 3 or invasive carcinoma during follow-up was classified as progression. For the analysis, persistence and progression were grouped into ≥ CIN2 (no regression). All included cases were reviewed by the most experienced colposcopist in the service to identify biopsy failures. When the lesion aspect was worsened, progression was considered. In cases of divergent diagnoses (cytopathological, histopathological, or colposcopic) on the same date, the histopathological diagnosis or the most severe (between cytology and colposcopy) was considered the outcome. Colposcopy Data from colposcopies prior to the initial biopsy and follow-up colposcopies were collected from specific forms and confirmed or completed from patient records. The previous colposcopy was considered the examination performed before the biopsy with a diagnosis of CIN2. Follow-up colposcopies were performed semiannually by experienced colposcopists at the cervical pathology unit. Colposcopy results were classified as normal findings, minor or major abnormal findings, or suggestive of invasion. Cytological and histopathological results Results were obtained from medical records based on cytology reports from different SUS primary care centers. Follow-up cytology was performed by the same cytopathologist from the cervical pathology reference center in RJ, and results were collected from reports attached to medical records. Histopathological results of the biopsies were confirmed by at least two pathologists, who were blinded to the clinical outcome. Histopathological results from excisional treatment were obtained from reports prepared by pathologists at the same cervical pathology reference center. Immunohistochemistry Archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded histological blocks were retrieved when available

abnormal findings, or suggestive of invasion. Cytological and histopathological results Results were obtained from medical records based on cytology reports from different SUS primary care centers. Follow-up cytology was performed by the same cytopathologist from the cervical pathology reference center in RJ, and results were collected from reports attached to medical records. Histopathological results of the biopsies were confirmed by at least two pathologists, who were blinded to the clinical outcome. Histopathological results from excisional treatment were obtained from reports prepared by pathologists at the same cervical pathology reference center. Immunohistochemistry Archived formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded histological blocks were retrieved when available and used for immunohistochemical analyses. All immunohistochemistry reactions were performed in a single laboratory, as part of this study, following the same protocol. Immunohistochemical expression of p16 was analyzed using a pre-diluted mouse monoclonal antibody anti-p16 (dilution 1:30; CINtec p16 Histology, Ventana Medical Systems, Tucson, USA) and a monoclonal anti-Ki-67 antibody (1:200 dilution; clone SP6, Cell Marque, Rocklin, USA, using the Max Polymer Detection System, BOND-MAX, Leica, Melbourne, Australia) using an automated system. As a positive control, TMA slides positive for p16 and Ki-67 were prepared according to the method developed by Pires et al. [ ]. For the negative control, the primary antibody was replaced by phosphate-buffered saline. Evaluation of Immunohistochemical staining At least two experienced pathologists classified p16 immunohistochemical staining according to the LAST recommendations: strong, diffuse staining in at least one-third of the epithelium was considered positive, whereas focal or multifocal weak or absent staining was considered negative. Consensus diagnosis among pathologists was considered for analysis. In case of disagreement, samples were re-evaluated together to define the classification of p16 immunohistochemical staining. Ki-67 staining was considered positive when more than 50% of cells in the lesion were stained, as determined by digital quantification. Slides were digitized using the Aperio ScanScope CS5 scanner (Leica, Vista, USA). Ki-67 expression was quantified using Aperio ImageScope software, version 11 (Leica, Vista, USA), using the IHC Nuclear algorithm, version 1 (Leica, Vista, USA), with the pathologist demarcating the quantification area. Statistical analysis Baseline characteristics are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) or as n (%). Age was dichotomized at 30 years, based on evidence that CIN2 regression rates are higher in women aged ≤30 years [ ]. Bivariate associations between baseline variables and lesion regression were examined using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. Crude odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported. For variables with sparse data or zero cells, odds ratios were not estimated due to instability of the estimates. Time-to-event analyses were performed using Kaplan-Meier curves to estimate the cumulative probability and median time to lesion regression and progression, with corresponding standard errors and 95% confidence intervals. Given the limited number of events and substantial censoring, multivariable time-to-event regression models were not performed. A two-sided p-value ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were conducted using SPSS version 20.0. In addition, a sensitivity analysis was conducted to assess potential differences in outcome distribution and biomarker status between patients included retrospectively from the institutional database and those enrolled prospectively. Ethical considerations The institution’s Research Ethics Committee approved the study under protocol number CAAE 76241617.4.0000.5269. Patients still under active surveillance provided consent at study initiation or at entry for prospectively enrolled cases. Patients who had already been discharged from follow-up had their consent waived. The data was accessed between 18 July 2018 and 31 May 2022, and only one of the authors had access to information that could identify individual participants during data collection. The colposcopists were responsible for treatment decisions based on patient history, cytology results, colposcopic impression, and patient preferences. Results A total of 173 women with a histopathological diagnosis of CIN2 were identified, comprising 127 cases from January 2006 to June 2018 and 46 cases from July 2018 to May 2022 ( ). After applying the exclusion criteria, 68 cases met eligibility criteria. Among these, 18 patients were considered lost to follow-up. Thus, 50 patients were included in the analysis of clinical outcomes and baseline characteristics. Of these, 38/50 (76%) had available p16 and Ki-67 immunohistochemistry, while 12 cases lacked biomarker data due to unavailable paraffin blocks or absence of residual lesion on deeper sections. At the end of the study, 76% (38/50; 95% CI: 64.2–87.8%) of cases showed regression, 12% (6/50; 95% CI: 3.0–21%) showed lesion persistence, and 12% (6/50; 95% CI: 3.0–21%) progressed to CIN 3 (5/6) or carcinoma (1/6). The case demonstrating progression to carcinoma was identified within the retrospective cohort; the patient had discontinued follow-up and returned five years after the initial diagnosis of CIN2. summarizes the baseline characteristics of the included CIN2 cases. The case demonstrating progression to carcinoma was identified within the retrospective cohort; the patient had discontinued follow-up and returned five years after the initial diagnosis of CIN2. summarizes the baseline characteristics of the included CIN2 cases. In one case, the initial colposcopy report could not be located. Twelve cases did not provide sufficient information on p16 and Ki-67 status due to a lack of paraffin blocks or the absence of CIN2 lesions in the immunohistochemical slides. The mean age of the study patients was 30.5 years, ranging from 17.7 to 48.9 years. Most patients were referred to colposcopy with a previous cytology result of HSIL (48%, 24/50), and 51% (25/49) of those cases had minor abnormal colposcopic findings. Immunohistochemical staining of p16 was considered positive in 81.6% (31/38) of cases, and Ki-67 was negative in 89.5% (34/38) of CIN2 biopsies analyzed. The median time between biopsy and outcome determination was 11.3 months, ranging from 3.7 to 60.2 months of follow-up. During the follow-up period, 38 (76%) patients showed regression, 6 (12%) showed persistence of the lesion, and 6 (12%) progressed to CIN 3 (5) or carcinoma (1). In regressor cases, the median clinical follow-up time was 9.8 months (4.2–32 months); for persistent cases, 12.6 months (3.7–28 months); and for progressing cases, 39.6 months (29.4–60.2 months). Among women with regression outcome, 79% (30/38) showed complete regression, and 21% (8/38) showed partial regression (regression up to CIN 1 or LSIL). For analysis, complete or partial regression was considered together. The Kaplan–Meier curves ( ) demonstrate distinct temporal patterns for CIN2 regression and progression. Most regression events occurred early in follow-up. Kaplan-Meier analysis showed that the median time to lesion regression was 357 days (standard error [SE] = 61.4 days; 95% CI: 236.6–477.4 days). In contrast, progression events accumulated more slowly and tended to appear later: Kaplan–Meier analysis showed a median time to progression of 966 days (SE = 159.1 days; 95% CI: 654.1–1277.9 days). presents the bivariate analysis of baseline characteristics and regression outcome. None of the evaluated variables showed a statistically significant association with regression. Still, the highest post-hoc statistical power observed was 24%, corresponding to the association between colposcopic findings and clinical outcomes. Sensitivity analyses showed no significant differences in the distribution of outcomes between retrospectively identified cases and prospectively enrolled patients (χ² = 3.986, p = 0.1363). Similarly, no differences were observed in the distribution of biomarker status across data collection modes (Fisher’s exact test, p16 p = 0.41; Ki-67 p = 0.29) ( ). Discussion This cohort study evaluated the natural history of biopsy-confirmed CIN2 managed conservatively in a middle-income country public healthcare setting, describing time to regression and progression, and exploring whether p16, Ki-67, age, referral cytology, or colposcopic findings were associated with regression. We found that 76% (38/50) of CIN2 patients experienced lesion regression. None of the baseline characteristics analyzed – including p16 status, Ki-67 status, age, referral cytology, or colposcopy findings – showed a statistically significant association with regression in bivariate analysis. Given the limited number of events, no multivariable time-to-event regression analyses were performed. Previous studies have reported that all progressive cases showed positive p16 staining, as per the LAST criteria [ , ]. Another study reported that 80% of cases that progressed were p16 positive [ ]. Some studies have found a statistically significant difference between p16 immunohistochemical staining classification and the evaluated outcomes [ , , ]. In our cohort, 81.6% (31/38) were p16-positive, and 71% of these cases experienced regression. There was no statistically significant association between p16 status and regression; however, our study lacked sufficient power to rule out such an association. Our study included only CIN2 biopsy-confirmed cases, as confirmed by at least two pathologists. Another cohort study, involving 443 women, found that when focusing solely on expert-confirmed CIN2 cases, the risk of regression did not vary based on p16 status [ ]. Similarly, Ki-67 status was not associated with regression. Again, our study lacked sufficient power to demonstrate that no such association exists conclusively. The high percentage (89%) of CIN2 “negative” for Ki-67 was unexpected and could partly be explained by the high (≥50% of stained cells) cut-off applied. This cut-off was chosen because it had been linked to progression in a previous study [ ]. Progression cases had a mean labeling index of 25.98% (range 13–39%), suggesting that our higher cut-off may partly explain the lack of association. Variability in sensitivity among Ki-67 antibody clones has also been documented in other settings [ ]. Other authors using different cut-offs have reported significant associations [ ]. Our results, therefore,

no such association exists conclusively. The high percentage (89%) of CIN2 “negative” for Ki-67 was unexpected and could partly be explained by the high (≥50% of stained cells) cut-off applied. This cut-off was chosen because it had been linked to progression in a previous study [ ]. Progression cases had a mean labeling index of 25.98% (range 13–39%), suggesting that our higher cut-off may partly explain the lack of association. Variability in sensitivity among Ki-67 antibody clones has also been documented in other settings [ ]. Other authors using different cut-offs have reported significant associations [ ]. Our results, therefore, do not diminish the potential value of p16 and Ki-67 as biomarkers; instead, they reflect limitations related to cut-off selection and sample size in the present study. The need for larger, standardized studies to confirm the predictive utility of these biomarkers—particularly in untreated CIN2 cohorts—has also been emphasized by a recent systematic review on predictive biomarkers of clinical evolution in conservatively managed patients [ ]. Our study, as well as others [ , ], found no significant difference in patient outcomes by age. However, this observation is likely influenced by limited statistical power to detect age-specific effects. Therefore, the lack of statistical significance does not exclude a potential biological role of age in the evolution of CIN2. Rather, it underscores the need for prospective studies assessing conservative management of CIN2, regardless of age, provided adequate follow-up is ensured. The median time to regression events was nearly 1 year (357 days; 95% CI: 236.6–477.4 days), but among cases that progressed, this period was about 3 times longer (966 days; SE: 159.1; 95% CI: 654.1–1277.9). The Kaplan-Meier curves demonstrated that regression is typically an early event, whereas progression tends to occur later. The probability of regression rose steeply within the first two to three years. It plateaued thereafter, while the cumulative probability of progression remained low during the first two years and increased gradually thereafter, with all progression events occurring after a two-year follow-up. This finding is partly due to the predetermined treatment time in persistent cases. These data suggest that a 24-month period of active surveillance is an appropriate and safe timeframe for the conservative management of CIN2, provided patients comply with follow-up protocols. Following this period, cases that do not regress should be re-evaluated to determine whether continued surveillance or treatment is necessary. This interpretation aligns with prior studies reporting regression rates of 64%−74% after 2 years of surveillance [ , ] and is consistent with the meta-analysis by Tainio et al. [ ], which supports conservative management. Despite some previous studies reporting no carcinoma cases in patients with CIN2 biopsies [ , ], our retrospective data identified one case (2%) of progression to carcinoma after five years from the initial diagnosis of CIN2. The patient had abandoned follow-up and returned three years later. Another cohort study reported six cases of progression to carcinoma (0.2%) [ ]. Their cases with this outcome had persistent lesions with high-grade cytology and/or previous high-risk HPV. Half of these patients were diagnosed with cancer and progressed after a 2- to 3-year interval in follow-up. A recent Danish cohort population-based study reported an increased long-term risk of cervical cancer for women undergoing active surveillance for CIN2 compared to those who received immediate surgical excision [ ]. These findings highlight the importance of continuing clinical follow-up for some time, even after regression, given the risk of lesion recurrence. Management of CIN2 depends on clinical factors and patient preferences, especially regarding obstetric risks. While excisional procedures are known to increase obstetric complications [ ], a recent cohort study showed similar preterm birth rates for active surveillance and immediate excision. Delayed excision, however, raised the risk of preterm birth by 30% compared to immediate surgery [ ]. However, the choice of clinical management in this group of patients remains a challenge, as histopathological results are still used as the gold standard. It is widely documented in the literature that the interpretation and reproducibility of biopsies are limited. In addition to low interobserver agreement, especially in cases of CIN2, this diagnostic category is also notoriously heterogeneous, including transient HPV lesions and lesions with progressive potential. For these reasons, interest in criteria or biomarkers that can predict and differentiate truly progressive lesions from regressive ones is increasing [ ]. Our study sought to minimize low interobserver reproducibility by including only CIN2 biopsy cases evaluated by at least two pathologists. Additionally, all cases were reassessed by an experienced colposcopist to determine outcomes, especially whether cases considered to be progression were truly CIN2 lesions that had progressed, or higher-grade lesions (CIN 3 and carcinoma) present on the cervix but not represented in the initial biopsy. in criteria or biomarkers that can predict and differentiate truly progressive lesions from regressive ones is increasing [ ]. Our study sought to minimize low interobserver reproducibility by including only CIN2 biopsy cases evaluated by at least two pathologists. Additionally, all cases were reassessed by an experienced colposcopist to determine outcomes, especially whether cases considered to be progression were truly CIN2 lesions that had progressed, or higher-grade lesions (CIN 3 and carcinoma) present on the cervix but not represented in the initial biopsy. These findings most likely reflect sampling error or underrepresentation of a higher-grade lesion at the time of biopsy (biopsy failure), rather than actual biological progression over such a short interval. These cases were excluded to avoid misclassification and to ensure that only actual CIN2 cases under conservative management were included in the analysis. Also, cases diagnosed by excisional biopsy were excluded to avoid outcome misclassification, as these lesions would be incorrectly classified as “regression” despite being physically removed rather than undergoing spontaneous biological regression. Inclusion of such cases would artificially inflate regression rates and distort the natural history under conservative management. However, our study has significant limitations. The limited sample size reduced statistical power, particularly for analyses exploring associations between immunohistochemical markers and lesion regression. Therefore, non-significant findings should not be interpreted as an absence of association. A larger, multicenter dataset will be necessary to evaluate predictive factors with adequate precision. This study included both retrospectively identified and prospectively enrolled patients, which may have introduced some heterogeneity related to data collection. However, all analyses were conducted using the same predefined protocols, and sensitivity analyses showed no significant differences in the distribution of outcomes or biomarker status between cohorts, suggesting that the bidirectional design is unlikely to have introduced substantial bias into the results. p16 and Ki-67 immunohistochemistry were not performed routinely in clinical practice and were assessed retrospectively for research purposes, depending on the availability and adequacy of archived biopsy material. Consequently, missing biomarker data were unlikely to be missing at random. Importantly, however, these missing data were not associated with clinical outcomes, suggesting a low risk of bias. In addition, immunohistochemical results were not used to guide clinical management and were evaluated solely to explore potential associations with clinical outcomes. The study reflects the Brazilian public healthcare system (SUS), in which cervical screening is opportunistic; generalizability to other settings with different screening infrastructures should be approached with caution. These limitations, particularly the small sample size, mean that our inability to detect predictive value for baseline characteristics does not rule out their potential importance. Despite the limited statistical power, this study provides a well-characterized cohort of women with biopsy-confirmed CIN2 cases managed conservatively under a standardized follow-up protocol. The prospective assessment of outcomes and the detailed clinical, histopathological, and immunohistochemical characterization contribute valuable real-world data from a public healthcare setting in a middle-income country. Importantly, by making these data openly available, this study aims to facilitate support for future pooled analyses and multicenter collaborations, in which larger sample sizes may allow more robust evaluation of potential predictive factors in CIN2 management. Conclusion In this study, CIN2 regression occurred in 76% of the included cases, with median times of approximately 12 months for regression and 32 months for progression. No statistically significant associations between baseline characteristics, including biomarkers, and lesion regression were observed in this cohort; however, the exploratory nature of the analysis, limited sample size, and substantial censoring preclude definitive conclusions. documents.title: ACOG Practice Bulletin Multifetal Gestations Twin Pregnancy Management

chunks.content: Abbreviations ART assisted reproductive technologies CVS chorionic villus sampling IUFD intrauterine fetal death NICU neonatal intensive care unit PPROM preterm pre‐labor rupture of membranes PTL preterm labor RFA radiofrequency ablation Key message Triplet gestations remain vulnerable to early loss and preterm birth. Appropriately timed fetal reduction improved perinatal outcomes in our cohort. These results strengthen evidence for individualized management strategies. 1 INTRODUCTION As the rate of assisted reproductive technologies (ART), such as in vitro fertilization, increases and maternal age rises, multifetal pregnancies have become more common worldwide. In Korea, while the overall birth rate continues to decline, the proportion of multiple births has steadily increased from 3.5% in 2014 to 5.5% in 2023. Multifetal pregnancies are associated with increased risks not only for infants—such as prematurity and cerebral palsy—but also for mothers, with higher rates of obstetric complications. The rate of cerebral palsy per 1000 live births increases from 1.6 in singleton pregnancies to 28 in triplet pregnancies, and infant mortality rises from 5.4 to 52.5 per 1000 live births. In response to these risks, fetal reduction procedures, including multifetal pregnancy reduction (MFPR) for reducing the number of fetuses and selective termination for confirmed congenital or chromosomal abnormalities, are increasingly being considered, while clinicians must navigate ethical, religious, and social concerns. Beginning in the late 1990s, numerous publications reported perinatal outcomes before and after fetal reduction, and by the early 2000s, several series reported improvements in fetal loss and early prematurity after fetal reduction. , Subsequent studies examined pregnancy loss, , and both single‐center and large multicenter series have demonstrated that overall pregnancy loss rates after MFPR have declined with increasing operator experience, stabilizing at approximately 4%–6%. , , Research has also highlighted the need to evaluate neonatal survival and long‐term outcomes. A 2010 review noted advances in the expectant management of triplet pregnancies with acceptable perinatal outcomes but also concluded that elective reduction to twins is associated with a lower risk of preterm birth without an increased risk of miscarriage. The existing literature has addressed not only the potential benefits of fetal reduction but also the procedure‐related risks, including overall pregnancy loss. However, controversy remains regarding the optimal management of triplet gestations. Accordingly, evidence‐based clinical guidance and patient counseling on the management and outcomes of triplet pregnancies have become increasingly important. In this study, we aimed to evaluate perinatal outcomes of triplet pregnancies and compare outcomes between pregnancies managed expectantly and those undergoing fetal reduction. 2 MATERIAL AND METHODS 2.1 Study design We retrospectively reviewed pregnant women with triplet pregnancies confirmed by ultrasound at Asan Medical Center between January 2020 and May 2025. Cases in which fetal reduction was performed, and the pregnancy was subsequently maintained as a twin or singleton, were also included. Patients who had not delivered at the time of analysis or were lost to follow‐up before the second trimester, with no subsequent data available at our institution, were excluded. We collected the following baseline characteristics: maternal age, height, body mass index (BMI), parity, history of preterm delivery, method of conception, presence of hypertensive diseases, pregestational diabetes, gestational diabetes mellitus, type of chorionicity, and use of invasive diagnostic tests, such as chorionic villus sampling (CVS) and amniocentesis. Perinatal outcomes included gestational age at delivery, delayed‐interval delivery, mode of delivery, procedure‐to‐delivery interval in cases undergoing intervention, and delivery before 28, 30, or 32 weeks of gestation. We defined unintended intrauterine death of at least one fetus before 24 weeks of gestation, as well as the loss of all fetuses before 24 weeks, as nonviable pregnancy loss. We also collected stillbirths occurring after 24 weeks. We recorded delivery‐related and obstetric complications, including McDonald cerclage, admission due to incompetent internal os of the cervix, preterm labor (PTL), and preterm pre‐labor rupture of membranes (PPROM), hypertensive complications, including preeclampsia and superimposed preeclampsia, and postpartum hemorrhage requiring ≥4 units of transfusion or surgical or nonsurgical intervention. Neonatal outcomes included sex, birth weight, 1‐ and 5‐min Apgar scores, need for oxygen therapy within the first 24 h after birth, admission to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU), and survival at 28 days of life. For cases undergoing fetal reduction, we additionally collected the following data: gestational age at the time of the procedure, type of procedure, indication for the procedure, medications used, need for repeat procedures, amnioreduction, duration of hospitalization, and any adverse events within 2 weeks post‐procedure, including PPROM, chorioamnionitis, intrauterine fetal demise, and PTL. All cases were assessed to determine whether fetal reduction had been performed. Cases in which all three fetuses were maintained without reduction were classified as the expectant management group, while those that underwent fetal reduction were classified as the fetal reduction group. Outcomes were compared between the two groups. Further sub‐analyses were conducted according to the indication and method of the procedure, comparing multifetal pregnancy reduction

procedure, type of procedure, indication for the procedure, medications used, need for repeat procedures, amnioreduction, duration of hospitalization, and any adverse events within 2 weeks post‐procedure, including PPROM, chorioamnionitis, intrauterine fetal demise, and PTL. All cases were assessed to determine whether fetal reduction had been performed. Cases in which all three fetuses were maintained without reduction were classified as the expectant management group, while those that underwent fetal reduction were classified as the fetal reduction group. Outcomes were compared between the two groups. Further sub‐analyses were conducted according to the indication and method of the procedure, comparing multifetal pregnancy reduction vs. selective fetal termination, and intracardiac injection vs. radiofrequency ablation (RFA). This study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of Asan Medical Center (IRB number: 2025‐0872). 2.2 Clinical practice and protocols for fetal reduction Fetal reduction was classified into two categories based on the indication: Multifetal pregnancy reduction and Selective Fetal Termination. Multifetal pregnancy reductio was performed to reduce the number of fetuses in a multifetal pregnancy, whereas selective fetal termination was performed when a structural anomaly or chromosomal abnormality was identified in one fetus. Although the indications differ, the procedural techniques were largely similar. In pregnancies without monochorionic (MC) twins, intracardiac injection of lidocaine or potassium chloride (KCl) was performed using a 21‐gauge needle under ultrasound guidance. In pregnancies involving MC twins, RFA was performed using a 15‐gauge LeVeen™ Needle Electrode (Boston Scientific, Marlborough, MA, USA) with a total length of 12 cm and a 2‐cm shunt to prevent hemodynamic complications in the co‐twin caused by placental vascular anastomoses. Peri‐procedural management was standardized. Patients were admitted on the day of the procedure, maintained fasting prior to intervention, and underwent fetal reduction under continuous ultrasound guidance. Follow‐up ultrasound examinations were performed on the day of the procedure and on the following day to assess the remaining fetal status and procedure‐related complications, after which patients were discharged if clinically stable. In this study, when a triplet pregnancy was diagnosed by ultrasound at the initial hospital visit, serum‐based screening tests were not routinely performed. First‐trimester screening was primarily based on nuchal translucency measurement, with invasive diagnostic testing offered when indicated. Following diagnosis of a triplet pregnancy, patients received counseling regarding the potential complications and obstetric outcomes associated with expectant management and fetal reduction. Management decisions were based on medical considerations and the patients' informed preferences. When fetal reduction was selected, genetic diagnostic testing, such as CVS, was recommended. CVS was routinely performed according to chorionicity, with one sampling in MC triplet pregnancies, two in dichorionic triplet pregnancies, and three in trichorionic triplet pregnancies. Genetic testing results and ultrasound findings were reviewed to determine the target fetus. If no structural or chromosomal abnormality was identified, reduction was performed on the fetus in the most accessible and technically safe position. 2.3 Statistical analysis SAS software for Windows, version 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC, USA), was used for statistical analysis. Percentages were calculated based on available cases for each variable, and denominators differed because of missing data. Variables were organized to analyze case characteristics. Categorical variables were compared using the chi‐squared test and Fisher's exact test, and continuous variables were compared using the two‐sample t ‐test or Wilcoxon rank‐sum test. Subgroup analyses were performed by dividing cases into the “intracardiac injection” and “RFA” groups, and comparisons were made between each subgroup and the expectant management group. An additional subgroup analysis divided cases into the Multifetal Pregnancy Reduction and Selective Fetal Termination groups. A two‐sided p ‐value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. 3 RESULTS A total of 208 triplet pregnancies were included in the analysis (Figure ). Baseline characteristics of the total cohort and of the expectant management group ( n = 133) and fetal reduction group ( n = 75) are summarized in Table . The mean gestational age at diagnosis of triplet pregnancy in the overall cohort was 12.1 ± 4.3 weeks. Mean maternal age was comparable between groups, whereas BMI was significantly higher in the expectant management group than in the fetal reduction group. Other demographic characteristics, including parity and height, did not differ significantly. 3.1 Natural course and outcomes in the EM group Of the 208 triplet pregnancies, 133 (63.9%) were managed expectantly without fetal reduction. In the expectant management group, the mean maternal age was 35.1 years, and only 5.3% of cases were spontaneous pregnancies; the remaining 94.7% conceived through ART. The most common types of triplet pregnancies were dichorionic triamniotic (DCTA) pregnancies (48.9%) and trichorionic triamniotic (TCTA) pregnancies (45.9%) (Table ). Early fetal loss before 24 weeks, involving the death of at least one fetus, occurred in 10 cases (7.8%). Among these, three pregnancies (2.3%) resulted in nonviable pregnancy loss due to the demise of all three fetuses. Two cases were delivered following PPROM at 22 and 17 weeks

managed expectantly without fetal reduction. In the expectant management group, the mean maternal age was 35.1 years, and only 5.3% of cases were spontaneous pregnancies; the remaining 94.7% conceived through ART. The most common types of triplet pregnancies were dichorionic triamniotic (DCTA) pregnancies (48.9%) and trichorionic triamniotic (TCTA) pregnancies (45.9%) (Table ). Early fetal loss before 24 weeks, involving the death of at least one fetus, occurred in 10 cases (7.8%). Among these, three pregnancies (2.3%) resulted in nonviable pregnancy loss due to the demise of all three fetuses. Two cases were delivered following PPROM at 22 and 17 weeks of gestation, and one case was delivered at 22 weeks due to spontaneous PTL. Among the remaining seven cases, intrauterine fetal death (IUFD) of one or two fetuses occurred between 14 and 21 weeks of gestation in five cases. Two cases involved the intrauterine demise of two MC diamniotic twin fetuses, resulting in continuation as singleton pregnancies. Excluding the five IUFD cases, two pregnancies delivered one fetus first, following PPROM. Stillbirth after 24 weeks occurred in two cases: one at 24 weeks and one at 31 weeks of gestation (Table ). The detailed antenatal course and outcomes in these 10 cases are summarized in Table . The mean gestational age at delivery was 33.2 weeks, and the cesarean delivery rate was 90.6%. In 21.0% of cases, delivery was preceded by PPROM. The rates of delivery before 28, 30, and 32 weeks were 6.0%, 9.7%, and 21.6%, respectively. Peripartum hypertensive complications occurred in 12.8% of pregnancies, and postpartum hemorrhage was observed in 18.7% (Table ). A total of 76.7% of newborns required admission to the NICU; however, the overall neonatal survival rate was 98.4% (Table ). 3.2 Expectant management versus fetal reduction A comparative analysis was conducted between 133 cases in the expectant management group and 75 in the fetal reduction group. Maternal characteristics were generally comparable between the two groups, with no statistically significant differences except for BMI, the incidence of maternal diabetic disorders, and the rate of CVS performed before the procedure. CVS was conducted in 82.7% of cases in the fetal reduction group, which was significantly higher than that in the expectant management group (Table ). Fetal reduction was performed at a mean gestational age of 16 weeks. The mean duration of hospital stay following the procedure was 2.8 days. Procedure‐related complications within 2 weeks after fetal reduction occurred in 4 of 75 pregnancies (5.3%). These complications included PPROM in two cases and PTL requiring treatment in two cases. No cases of chorioamnionitis were observed. Neither PPROM nor PTL resulted in fetal demise (Table ). No cases of unexpected fetal loss or stillbirth were observed in the fetal reduction group. No cases of nonviable pregnancy loss occurred in the fetal reduction group, whereas such losses occurred in 2.3% of cases in the expectant management group. The incidence of preterm birth before 32 weeks of gestation was 21.6% (24/111) in the expectant management group and 11.4% (5/44) in the fetal reduction group. However, because of the significant proportion of missing data for this outcome, these findings should be interpreted with caution (Table ). The mean birth weight of neonates was higher in the fetal reduction group (2157.0 ± 529.5 g) than in the expectant management group (1816.5 ± 439.4 g, p < 0.0001). The 1‐ and 5‐min Apgar scores were also significantly higher in the fetal reduction group (7.9 ± 1.4 and 9.0 ± 0.9, respectively) than in the expectant management group (7.1 ± 1.8 and 8.3 ± 1.5, respectively; p < 0.0001 for both). The proportion of neonates requiring oxygen therapy within the first 24 h after delivery was significantly lower in the fetal reduction group (18.4%) than in the expectant management group (50.2%, p < 0.0001). The rate of NICU admission was significantly lower in the fetal reduction group (34.6%) than in the expectant management group (76.7%, p < 0.0001). Survival rates were high in both groups, with no statistically significant difference (98.4% in expectant management vs. 100% in fetal reduction, p = 0.5770). Perinatal outcomes of DCTA and TCTA triplet pregnancies, which constituted the majority of the cohort, are summarized in Table . In this cohort, especially within the expectant management group, DCTA triplets demonstrated a higher rate of loss of ≥1 fetus before 24 weeks of gestation, including nonviable pregnancy loss, compared with TCTA triplets. Given the rarity and heterogeneity of less common triplet types, their individual clinical courses and perinatal outcomes are presented in Table . 3.3 Results of subanalysis Within the fetal reduction group, outcomes were compared between procedures performed using intracardiac injection ( n = 49) and RFA ( n = 26) (Figure ). The mean gestational age at the time of the procedure was slightly earlier in the intracardiac injection group

especially within the expectant management group, DCTA triplets demonstrated a higher rate of loss of ≥1 fetus before 24 weeks of gestation, including nonviable pregnancy loss, compared with TCTA triplets. Given the rarity and heterogeneity of less common triplet types, their individual clinical courses and perinatal outcomes are presented in Table . 3.3 Results of subanalysis Within the fetal reduction group, outcomes were compared between procedures performed using intracardiac injection ( n = 49) and RFA ( n = 26) (Figure ). The mean gestational age at the time of the procedure was slightly earlier in the intracardiac injection group (15.9 ± 4.2 weeks) than in the RFA group (16.3 ± 1.0 weeks); however, the difference was not statistically significant ( p = 0.5029) (Table ). No significant differences were observed between the two groups in the need for reintervention or duration of hospital stay. Notably, while no cases of PPROM occurred in the intracardiac injection group, two cases (7.7%) occurred in the RFA group within 2 weeks post‐procedure; however, this difference did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.1111). Another subgroup analysis was performed within the fetal reduction group, comparing 53 cases of multifetal pregnancy reduction and 22 cases of selective fetal termination (Table ). The mean gestational age at the time of the procedure was significantly earlier in the multifetal pregnancy reduction group (15.2 ± 3.0 weeks) than in the selective fetal termination group (18.0 ± 3.8 weeks, p = 0.0008). Despite this difference in timing, no statistically significant differences were observed in adverse events within 2 weeks post‐procedure between the two groups. 4 DISCUSSION In this study, we analyzed the natural course of triplet pregnancies according to management strategy. Among triplet pregnancies managed expectantly, the rate of fetal loss involving at least one fetus before 24 weeks was 7.8%, and the incidence of nonviable pregnancy loss was 2.3%. The mean gestational age at delivery was approximately 33.2 weeks, and postpartum hemorrhage occurred in 18.7% of cases. In contrast, pregnancies that underwent fetal reduction demonstrated overall more favorable perinatal outcomes. The procedure‐related complication rate was approximately 5%, and no cases of nonviable pregnancy loss occurred before 24 weeks of gestation. Notably, neonatal outcomes were better in the fetal reduction group, with significantly lower rates of NICU admission and oxygen requirement. These findings support the safety and efficacy of fetal reduction when appropriately indicated. In the expectant management cases, the rate of nonviable pregnancy loss before 24 weeks was slightly higher (2.3% vs. 1.1%) than the rate reported in a recent cohort. Compared with that report, which noted single and double IUFD rates of 18.2% and 9.1%, respectively, after 24 weeks of gestation, the stillbirth rate of 1.9% in our cohort suggests a relatively favorable outcome. Several studies have reported fetal loss rates before 24 weeks ranging from 7.3% to 13.3%. , , A 2015 systematic review also reported a pregnancy loss rate of 9.3%. Another, more recent systematic review reported a higher pregnancy loss rate, further highlighting the comparatively lower rate observed in our study. These findings are relatively favorable compared with previous reports; however, the risk of pregnancy loss remains a clinically significant concern in the expectant management of triplet pregnancies. Regarding preterm birth, the rate of delivery before 32 weeks in the expectant management group was 21.6%, which is somewhat lower than previous reports showing rates of 26%–27.9%. , Compared with data from the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, which reported a mean gestational age at delivery of 31.7 weeks for triplet pregnancies, our cohort delivered at a slightly later mean gestational age of 33.0 weeks. These findings may partly reflect advancements in perinatal care over time, contributing to improved outcomes in more recent cohorts. The rate of preterm birth before 32 weeks in the expectant management group was slightly lower than previously reported rates; however, it still represents a significant risk. This underscores the persistent challenge of reducing preterm birth in triplet pregnancies, despite progressive improvements in obstetric and neonatal care. Regarding fetal reduction, the overall timing of the procedure was approximately 16.0 weeks of gestation, with the multifetal pregnancy reduction subgroup showing a mean gestational age of 15.2 weeks. The timing of fetal reduction in this cohort occurred relatively later than the 10+0 to 13+6 weeks generally recommended in earlier literature. , This delay likely resulted from the high frequency of CVS performed before the procedure, which allowed fetal selection based on comprehensive genetic and structural evaluation. fetal reduction in this cohort occurred relatively later than the 10+0 to 13+6 weeks generally recommended in earlier literature. , This delay likely resulted from the high frequency of CVS performed before the procedure, which allowed fetal selection based on comprehensive genetic and structural evaluation. Despite the advanced gestational age at the time of the procedure, no cases of fetal loss occurred before 24 weeks of gestation, and the overall rate of procedure‐related complications remained low. However, the absence of pregnancy loss following fetal reduction in this cohort should be interpreted with caution and does not necessarily indicate a protective effect of the procedure itself. Rather, this observation may reflect certain factors such as performance at an experienced fetal therapy center, careful patient selection, standardized procedural techniques, and close post‐procedural surveillance. In addition, the relatively small number of cases in the fetal reduction group raises the possibility that this finding may, at least in part, be attributable to chance. Therefore, these results should not be generalized and warrant confirmation in larger, multicenter studies. Subgroup analyses by indication and method of fetal reduction showed broadly consistent outcomes, with a low incidence of post‐procedural complications across subgroups. Neonatal outcomes appeared favorable across different approaches. These findings are consistent with the notion that fetal reduction, when appropriately indicated and carefully selected, may be considered as a management option to optimize outcomes in triplet pregnancies. Neonatal outcomes appeared favorable across different approaches; however, these findings should also be interpreted cautiously, given the limited sample sizes. Taken together, the subgroup results are consistent with the notion that fetal reduction, when appropriately indicated and performed in experienced centers, may be considered as one of the management options in selected triplet pregnancies. Notably, most triplet pregnancies in this cohort resulted from ART. Although fetal reduction may mitigate some risks associated with higher‐order multiple pregnancies, prevention remains the most effective strategy. Ongoing efforts to promote single embryo transfer and to limit the number of embryos transferred during ART cycles are therefore essential to reduce the incidence of triplet pregnancies. This study has certain limitations. First, not all women delivered at the same tertiary center where the fetal reduction was performed. Therefore, missing outcome data for some variables may limit the accuracy of the findings, and this factor should be considered when interpreting the results. Second, the relatively small sample size may reduce the statistical power of the analysis because the data were collected retrospectively, and some cases were lost to follow‐up, resulting in a limited number of cases included in each analysis. Despite these limitations, this study provides valuable data on recent outcomes of triplet pregnancies in Korea and offers important insight into perinatal outcomes following fetal reduction. Moreover, as this study included MC triplet pregnancies in which the reduction was performed using RFA, it uniquely encompasses outcomes across different reduction techniques, adding to its strength and novelty. Outcomes in the natural course of triplet pregnancies appear to be improving with advances in perinatal care; however, the risk of fetal loss remains. Fetal reduction, when appropriately indicated and performed at the optimal time, may prolong gestation and improve neonatal outcomes. These findings support fetal reduction as a viable management option and provide a foundation for individualized counseling in the management of triplet pregnancies. 5 CONCLUSION Triplet pregnancies are inherently associated with significant maternal and neonatal risks, even under expectant management. Our findings highlight that adverse outcomes, including early fetal loss, preterm birth, and peripartum complications, remain frequent in the natural course of triplet gestations. Fetal reduction, when considered in the context of triplet pregnancies, appears to be a relatively safe procedure and may be discussed as a management option in selected cases. It has the potential to prolong gestation and improve neonatal outcomes. These results underscore the importance of individualized counseling and a personalized prenatal approach when managing triplet pregnancies.
